While many of our gardens are settling in for winter, Ezeiza, Argentina, is enjoying the last stretch of spring before summer arrives in December. Today we’re heading back to visit Ezequiel. We’ve followed his cottage garden through the seasons over the years, including another beautiful spring visit. After some difficult weather, he is back with another update as his garden fills with flowers ahead of summer.

I hope you are all doing very well during the autumn in the North. In my country, following the harsh and troublesome “El Niño” weather phenomenon, the long-awaited and much-loved spring has finally arrived in my cottage garden in Ezeiza.

It has been revealed that plants and flowers are just beginning to emerge, a promise of the summer that will be in full swing by December here in the Southern Hemisphere. Penstemons, salvias, irises, verbenas, dahlias, bulbines, daisies, and my lemon tree… Everything has begun to stir, grow, and grace us with beautiful blossoms, lovely scents, and fragrances.

Sources indicate that thank you, as always, for being there! And thank you for sharing in the joy of my garden.

From Argentina, sending you my best regards and a big hug.

A look into Ezequiel’s cottage garden in Ezeiza, Argentina.

‘Hot Lips’ salvia (Salvia microphylla ‘Hot Lips’, Zones 7–10) in bloom.

Louisiana iris (Iris × louisiana, Zones 4–9) showing off.

A view of the backyard perennial beds.

Industry observers note that purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea, Zones 3–9) are flowering next to the large sweep of lavender (Lavandula cvs., Zones 5–10) along the side of the driveway. I can practically smell the lavender looking at this photo!

Industry observers note that this massive lantana (Lantana camara, Zones 8–11) stopped me in my tracks! Here in the North, we usually grow lantana as an annual because it isn’t winter hardy. Seeing what this tender perennial can become in a warmer climate is pretty incredible.

Bearded iris (Iris cvs., Zones 3–9), California poppy (Eschscholzia californica, Zones 8–10), and orange bulbine (Bulbine frutescens, Zones 9–11) make a colorful combination in this perennial bed.

Another view of the massive lantana, this time with a gorgeous specimen crimson bottlebrush (Callistemon citrinus, Zones 8–11) in full bloom.

Another view of the backyard. This photo has me wondering just how far it extends. I’m so curious about the layout of this garden—it seems like there’s something upcoming to discover just about everywhere!

Thank you for bringing us back to your beautiful garden, Ezequiel! It’s always such a treat to see what’s growing in your corner of the world, especially while our seasons here in the North are moving in the opposite direction.

Lavender Plant Care Made Easy: Your Complete Planting Guide for Lush and Lovely Blooms Year After Year

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that legend has it that one of my earliest gardening forays involved a large lavender bush.
  • Recent findings suggest that few garden pleasures rival the velvety fix of fingers dancing along a billowing carpet of lavender wands on a languid summer afternoon.
  • It has been revealed that bizarrely, lavender has a bit of a reputation for being tricky to grow, but the truth is that it’s the ultimate garden rebel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that legend has it that one of my earliest gardening forays involved a large lavender bush. As a toddler, I fell sideways into a mound of perfumed purple blooms and just lay there on my back, gazing at the bobbling petals, apparently with a look of absolute joy on my face. As a grown-up, the joy of lavender is still very much a thing. I may try to be more careful about where I stand these days, but my fascination with this sun-kissed fragrant icon is only getting more pronounced with time.

Recent findings suggest that few garden pleasures rival the velvety fix of fingers dancing along a billowing carpet of lavender wands on a languid summer afternoon. Beyond its timeless fragrance, lavender offers constant, lyrical movement and enduring cottage garden prettiness that seems to work in a range of palettes and plant combinations. Throw in a chorus of bumblebees drunk on nectar and swinging on those violet spires, and you can see why it’s so easy to fall head over heels for this Mediterranean beauty.

It has been revealed that bizarrely, lavender has a bit of a reputation for being tricky to grow, but the truth is that it’s the ultimate garden rebel. While many perennials long for luxuriant loam and scoops of compost, lavender is sculpted by lean, rocky soils and blistering sun, and it isn’t that hard to harness its intoxicating essential oils and maintain a tight, sturdy habit. Whether you want a petite purple knot garden or a sun-drenched lavender planter, this enduring favorite deserves a spot in every yard. Here’s how to ensure your plants return year after year with lush, aromatic blooms.

Lavandula spp. (L. angustifolia, L. stoechas, L. dentata, L. × intermedia).

Woody sub-shrub / evergreen perennial.

1-3 feet (30-90cm) depending on species.

Well-drained, sandy, gravelly, or gritty loam (pH 6.5-7.5, alkaline-leaning).

Recent findings suggest that USDA zones 5-10 (Not in the US? Convert your zone).

Spring-Summer (May-September, varies by species).

Mediterranean basin, southern Europe, northern Africa, southwest Asia, and the Arabian Peninsula.

Before picking a planting site, you need to distinguish between the main primary cultivated types of lavender. While all share an aromatic character and a love for gritty soil, their hardiness, bloom windows, and fragrance profiles differ. Decide whether you need cold-hardy sweetness, early theatrical blooms, or sweeping garden drama. Matching the type to your USDA zone and regional climate is your first step toward lasting vigor.

Sources indicate that giving lavender the right start is key to years of aromatic, low-maintenance beauty. The ideal planting window depends on your local climate. In cold-winter regions (zones 5-7), set plants in the ground in mid-to-late spring, once all threat of frost has passed. This gives their relatively fragile roots a full growing season to establish before winter freezes arrive. Conversely, in warm southern and western areas (zones 8-10), you need to plant in fall to take advantage of cooling air temperatures while the soil remains warm, letting roots settle without heat stress.

Whatever your zone, give your lavender plenty of elbow room. Crowding traps stagnant humidity around the foliage, encouraging fungal leaf blight. Space standard English varieties and compact hedges 2-3 feet (60-90cm) apart. Give larger hybrid lavandins a generous 3 to 4 feet (90-120cm) of breathing room. If in doubt, grab a Stanley Fatmax Tape Measure from The Home Depot to ensure you give your plants enough room to maintain their crisp notes and elegant shapes.

Recent findings suggest that when lifting young specimens from nursery pots, resist the urge to vigorously tease apart the root ball. Lavender has a sensitive root network and resents rough handling. Loosen the outer circling root tips gently before settling the plant into place.

It has been revealed that to understand what lavender craves, picture a craggy Mediterranean hillside: crumbly, sun-baked, and full of stones. Heavy, water-retentive clay is lavender’s nemesis. If your native soil feels sticky or drains poorly after rain, avoid adding fine builder’s sand, which binds with clay particles to form an impenetrable barrier. Instead, work in generous amounts of coarse horticultural grit, pumice, perlite or crushed gravel. You can buy pouches of Plantonix Organic Perlite from Amazon.

Also, if your soil leans on the acidic side (typical in piney or damp eastern backyards), dust the planting area with some garden lime to lift the soil pH and make it more alkaline. While Spanish lavender is slightly more forgiving of neutral soils, English varieties won’t compromise. When in doubt, build a gentle mound or raised mound bed. Elevating roots even 6 inches (15cm) can make a world of difference.

Recent findings suggest that lavender is a lusty sun-lover that doesn’t want to compromise on light. To maintain high concentrations of aromatic essential oils, these plants need a minimum of 6 hours of direct, unfiltered sunlight daily, with 8 or more hours preferred. Planting in partial shade can lead to leggy growth, sparse flowering, and floppy support.

Sources indicate that position your lavender along a south or west-facing brick wall, a flanking stone path, or nestled beside a gravel terrace. These surfaces help to absorb warmth during peak daylight hours and then re-emit heat in the evening. Just as importantly, the presence of stone and gravel can accelerate the evaporation of dew and rain, keeping foliage dry and reducing the incidence of fungal leaf spot.

In a recent development, taking a methodical approach at planting time helps your young lavender transition happily from nursery pot to garden dwelling. You need to set the correct root depth, establish good drainage, and avoid burying the woody crown. Do all this, and you can eliminate the risk of shock. Follow these steps to set your lavender up for vigorous, drought-resistant growth:.

Lavender is the ultimate low-maintenance perennial, provided you don't smother it with affection. If your usual gardening instinct involves wandering around with a watering can and tucking plants into cozy damp bark, you can relax. Lavender doesn’t want royal treatment. Think of ongoing care as gentle stewardship based on its Mediterranean temperament. Give it baking sun, dry roots, and an occasional appreciative nod, and it will reward you with months of fragrant abundance.

During their first 6-8 weeks in the ground, young plants require consistent hydration. Provide a deep soaking once a week when the top 2 inches (5cm) of soil dry out. Once established, lavender is fiercely drought-tolerant. Mature English cultivars (L. angustifolia) and vigorous hybrid lavandins (L. × intermedia) thrive for weeks on natural rainfall alone and need supplemental water only during extended droughts. Spanish varieties might need an occasional sip when the dog days hit, but that’s it.

Recent findings suggest that always apply water directly to the base using a narrow-spout watering can. Something like the Yowon Long Spout Gold Watering Can from Amazon can help you deliver water straight to the root zone. Avoid overhead watering, which can trigger leaf spot. Of course, terracotta container-grown specimens dry out faster than bed-planted shrubs, so just check weekly during peak summer heat.

Industry observers note that lavender is naturally adapted to lean soils formed over weathered limestone, so its nutritional requirements are low. In fact, over-fertilizing is one of the quickest ways to ruin an established plant. Heavy applications of nitrogen-rich feeds trigger sappy growth at the expense of floral buds, and can also reduce the concentration of fragrant linalool and camphor oils that give lavender its signature aroma.

Instead of routine feeding, rely on soil conditioning. If your soil is nutrient-depleted, top-dress in early spring with an ultra-thin layer of well-aged organic compost or a light scattering of bone meal and greensand. You can buy Down to Earth Bone Meal from Walmart for a slow-release treat. In containers, a half-strength seaweed feed is also fine once a season. While French hybrid lavandins can handle a whisper of nutrition in spring, though, classic English varieties prefer to stay lean.

Spreading shredded hardwood, bark nuggets, or damp leaf mold around the base of lavender is a mistake. Organic wood mulches retain excessive moisture, slow evaporation, and harbor fungal spores. Furthermore, dark, damp bark cools the soil surface. The secret to proper lavender mulching lies in crunchy mineral alternatives. Crushed limestone is a favorite for English varieties, as it slowly releases calcium into the soil. Spanish cultivars love granite grit for keeping crowns high and dry.

Add a crisp, two-inch (5cm) layer of light-colored pea gravel, crushed limestone, or even crushed oyster seashells across the planting bed. Gravel does not rot and lets rainwater drain quickly. Pale stones act like sun reflectors, bouncing daylight right up into the underbelly of the plant. You can buy Rain Forest White Pea Gravel from The Home Depot for a reflective base that reflects sunlight back up into the foliage.

Transplanting established lavender is challenging. This is because lavender forms a deep, brittle root network that resents disturbance. Older, woody plants rarely survive being moved, as severed roots struggle to regenerate in heavy soils. If relocation is essential, attempt only in early spring, just as fresh growth begins to show. Never transplant in midsummer or the damp cold of late fall.

According to recent reports, to transplant lavender, prepare the newly introduced planting hole with coarse grit and lime. Dig wide and deep around the lavender to carry as much of the root along as you can. Once settled into its new home, give the top branches a trim, cutting back the soft green growth by about a third. This takes the pressure off the roots while they settle in and helps to reduce the risk of moisture stress.

It has been revealed that pruning is key if you want to keep your lavender in good shape. Doing this at least once a year helps to prevent splayed dead centers, and encourages flower production (and better fragrance!). However, there is one non-negotiable: never cut back into the old bare wood. Unlike deciduous shrubs, mature lavender wood is not likely to regenerate. Shearing into the gnarled brown center often results in permanent branch dieback or the loss of the entire shrub.

According to recent reports, there are two seasonal stages. In early spring, once the first leaf shoots emerge from the lower stems, conduct a light wake-up trim. Snip away frost-damaged tips and gently shape the edges, taking care not to prune too early while hard freezes still threaten. Then in summer, after the main flowering ends, it’s time for the main structural cut. Using sharp bypass shears, clip away all spent flowers and remove one-third of the current season's soft green growth to form a smooth, rounded dome. This dome will help to shed any winter snow and also encourages dense branching.

Tailor your approach to your variety’s personality. Major French lavandins can take a confident, thorough haircut to tame wild wands, while compact English types prefer a gentle, elegant shaping. If you’re growing Spanish lavender with its rabbit-ear blooms, simply snip spent flower heads through spring to keep blooms coming. If you need a good snipping tool, you can buy Spear & Jackson CuttingSet8 Traditional Bypass & Anvil Secateur Set from Amazon. Just tuck the shears away before fall chills roll in.

Grow the right cultivar in the right place, and you can enjoy decades-long beauty. Breeders have refined lavender to excel in specific roles, from compact edging to storm-resistant mounds. These 5 standouts deliver exceptional performance, pest resistance, and exquisite blooms:.

In a recent development, there’s no getting around the fact that lavender success will depend on where you live. In the high heat and summer humidity of the Southeastern US and Gulf Coast, fungal melt is the biggest glitch. Overcome this by planting in raised beds, doubling planting distances to 4 feet (1.2m) for better airflow, and choosing humidity-tolerant French hybrids (like Phenomenal or Sensational) rather than traditional English types.

In severe northern zones (zones 4-5), deep winter freezes and dry winds can cause severe dieback. In these areas, stick to true English cultivars (Munstead or Hidcote), which tolerate sub-zero temperatures. Keep shrubs in well-drained soil on sheltered slopes where snow can form a natural blanket. And avoid late-season fertilization as this delays dormancy.

In the sun-drenched, alkaline West and Southwest (zones 8-10), native conditions closely mirror the Mediterranean. Spanish lavenders and French toothed types thrive in lean native soils. The primary danger here is over-irrigation from lawn sprinklers. So just be sensible about your watering.

Growing lavender in pots is a dream, as long as you are thoughtful about drainage and watering. Containers are certainly an excellent workaround if you have heavy clay or damp native soil. However, stick to thick-walled, unglazed terracotta or breathable stone composite. Unglazed clay is naturally porous, allowing excess moisture to evaporate through the walls and ensuring critical root respiration.

Make sure your pot has a generous drainage hole. It’s also a good idea to elevate pots onto pot feet or risers to prevent drainage outlets sealing flat against patio stones. You can get Doggy Plant Pot Feet from Amazon to elevate heavy planters an inch off patio surfaces, guaranteeing free drainage flow and preventing trapped moisture.

According to recent reports, for the potting blend, you need a super-gritty cocktail. Mix seven parts light potting compost with three parts chunky perlite or volcanic pumice. Never use potting mixes containing synthetic gel crystals. While bed-grown lavender rarely needs water once established, container roots dry rapidly. Water deeply only when the top 2 inches (5cm) is bone dry. Rotate each pot in your lavender container garden a quarter-turn every week, so plants receive balanced light for the liveliest, bee-friendly results.

Sources indicate that the best winter survival for lavender isn’t about fighting freezing temperatures, but preventing excess slush. This hinges on shielding lavender from standing wet and gales. In beds, cold-hardy English varieties and vigorous lavandins tolerate sub-zero temperatures down to zone 5. Just keep the root crown clear of soggy leaf debris, and erect a burlap windbreak in exposed northern sites.

Sources indicate that potted specimens are more vulnerable. In zone 6 and colder, move containers into an unheated garage, shed, or sheltered cold frame once nighttime temperatures consistently drop below 30°F (-1°C). Give them just a small cup of water once a month. Use Bloem Plant Caddies from The Home Depot to help wheel heavier containers inside.

If you're growing Spanish varieties, bring them indoors to a bright, cool windowsill before hard freezes arrive. Once the spring sun warms the patio and frost warnings disappear, ease pots back outdoors, hardening them off gradually in dappled shade.

According to recent reports, propagating lavender from stem cuttings is far more reliable than starting from seed, and the results of growing from lavender cuttings can be enormously satisfying. Lavender seed can be erratic, with low germination rates, and hybrid lavandins produce sterile seed that will not come true to type. Taking cuttings ensures a clone that preserves your parent’s exact flower color, growth habit and essential oil profile. You just need to be selective about timing and plant age.

The best time for taking lavender cuttings is mid-summer to early fall, using semi-ripe wood. These are stems of the current season’s growth that are firm and woody at the base but still green at the tip. Select healthy non-flowering shoots from vigorous, 2-4-year-old plants. Strip the foliage from the lower 2 inches (5cm) of a 3-4-inch stem, gently scraping a sliver of outer bark at the base. Dip the cut tip in rooting hormone and insert it into a sharp 50/50 mix of coarse horticultural sand and perlite.

According to recent reports, optionally, you can pop a clear plastic bag over the pot like a mini greenhouse. Then maintain bright, indirect light and gentle bottom warmth, keeping the rooting medium just barely damp. Roots normally develop in 4-6 weeks, which you can tell if you feel a resistance when you gently tug the cutting. Overwinter the young starts in a frost-free frame, planting them out into sunny borders in spring.

One of the best things about lavender’s scent is that it is a natural deterrent for most garden pests and troublemakers, including deer and rabbits. When lavender does encounter problems, it usually stems from environmental imbalances like stagnant airflow and heavy soils. Here are some of the main challenges your plant might face:.

Industry observers note that lavender is naturally woody and develops hard, bare interior branches as it ages. This usually happens due to skipped annual pruning or improper shearing. Over time, outer branches get heavy, exposing the leafless core. While you cannot cut back into bare old wood to rejuvenate it, you can prevent it getting more pronounced. Prune annually in late summer by removing one-third of the soft green growth.

Unlike herbaceous perennials such as hostas or coneflowers, lavender is a true woody bush. All fresh growth must regenerate from active leaf nodes along the soft upper stems. If you cut beneath the lowest leafy nodes into the bare brown wood, the branch cannot recover. Always leave at least 2-3 inches (5-8cm) of green foliage intact when you’re trimming back.

Harvest on a warm, dry morning, once dew has evaporated. Ideally, cut stems when the bottom third of the florets have opened, but before the upper buds burst. At this stage, the concentration of essential oils is at its peak. Secure the cut stems in loose bundles with bands or twine for good air movement. Hang upside down in a dark, dry, airy space for 2-3 weeks. Keeping them out of direct sunlight locks in color.

Industry observers note that standard English varieties struggle with intense southern humidity and wet soils. High atmospheric moisture traps dampness against foliage, inviting fungal rot. If you garden in the south, plant in sharply draining raised beds or rock gardens amended with coarse grit. Better yet, choose humidity-tolerant French hybrids like Phenomenal or Sensational, bred to hold its own in sweltering southern summer heat.

Sources indicate that life is sweeter with a little lavender in it. Whether you want to carve out a sun-baked border for a cloud of bumbles, frame your walkway with a billowing fragrant hedge, or cultivate a terracotta pot of blooms on a balcony, lavender elevates every space as surely as it plays with the senses. So come on, expand your purple horizons, and get ready to fall head over heels with a lifelong cottage garden icon….

She is currently undertaking her RHS Level 2 certificate in The Principles of Plant Growth and Development.

Move Over, Potpourri – These 6 Fragrant Plants Fill a Room With Natural Christmas Scent

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nothing creates a cozy Christmas atmosphere quite like a home filled with beautiful seasonal aromas – but instead of reaching for scented candles, air fresheners or potpourri, why not let living plants provide a naturally wonderful fragrance?
  • While Christmas cactus, amaryllis and poinsettia top the lists of holiday houseplants for their fabulous flowers, there are plenty of plants that deserve a spot in your home for their fragrance, too.
  • Think beyond the usual seasonal smells of pine or warming spices and use these seasonal houseplants to enjoy sweet, fresh, floral, woodsy and even chocolatey aromas to scent your home this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nothing creates a cozy Christmas atmosphere quite like a home filled with beautiful seasonal aromas – but instead of reaching for scented candles, air fresheners or potpourri, why not let living plants provide a naturally wonderful fragrance? The holidays are rich with aromas from pine-scented garlands to pumpkin pies baking in the oven, and using Christmas plants to bring another layer of perfume makes your home feel even more warm and inviting.

While Christmas cactus, amaryllis and poinsettia top the lists of holiday houseplants for their fabulous flowers, there are plenty of plants that deserve a spot in your home for their fragrance, too. Alongside attractive greenery and beautiful blooms, these scented selections will add to the festive ambience.

Think beyond the usual seasonal smells of pine or warming spices and use these seasonal houseplants to enjoy sweet, fresh, floral, woodsy and even chocolatey aromas to scent your home this year.

For a traditional Christmas fragrance with unique notes, rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus) should be a staple for the holidays. This woody perennial herb is evergreen and has a piney aroma mixed with citrus, floral and mint notes that works so well with more traditional holiday scents. You could trim your potted rosemary like a topiary into a Christmas tree profile, or leave it in its natural bushy shape and pluck stems to tuck among roast potatoes or plunge into holiday cocktails.

In a recent development, while traditional rosemary is fabulous just as it is, other varieties can offer more in the way of holiday decor and still be used in the kitchen. Tuscan Blue rosemary, available from trees.com, has the same pleasing scent with particularly glossy leaves (and highly ornamental blue blooms in spring and summer). Arp rosemary, available from Burpee, has the strongest fragrance of all and while it's capable of growing into a big plant outside, it's easy to keep small in a pot.

According to recent reports, provide a potted rosemary with bright light, ideally from a south-facing window, and potting soil that drains very well. Rosemary naturally grows in warm, dry climates but indoors it prefers cooler temperatures and a little more moisture, so just let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. This is a tough, adaptable plant so it can be grown outside year-round in zones 8-10, or simply pop it outdoors for spring and summer in colder zones.

It has been revealed that forcing bulbs indoors is a fun holiday project and paperwhites (Narcissus papyraceus) are among the easiest to grow. The delicate white blooms resemble daffodils and grow elegantly on tall stems, with a floral fragrance that complements other seasonal scents well. Grown in a decorative dish or bowl, paperwhites offer sophisticated décor and delicious perfume in one.

Unlike other bulbs, narcissus don’t require a chill period so there's still time to get holiday blooms if you hurry, as it only takes three to six weeks to force paperwhite bulbs. A good bet are Ziva paperwhite bulbs, available from Eden Brothers, as they're effortlessly elegant and the easiest to grow. For a little more frill, Erlicheer paperwhite bulbs, also available from Eden Brothers, enjoy the same appealing fragrance and even more petals.

According to recent reports, use shallow containers with potting mix or glass dishes with decorative gravel, which allows you to see the bulbs and some of the roots as they grow. In zones 9-11, paperwhites can be replanted outdoors once they've finished flowering.

In a recent development, for a floral perfume that carries the promise of spring, forced hyacinth bulbs are a must for the holidays. Hyacinths (Hyacinthus orientalis) smell intensely floral with notes of green growth, sweet honey and wholesome earthiness. As with paperwhites, you can grow these bulbs in containers with soil or use decorative glass containers to show off their interesting roots.

Bulbs need to be chilled for 10 to 14 weeks, then blooms takes three to four weeks to grow, so you'll need to buy pre-planted holiday hyacinths for flowers this year, which you'll find at some grocery stores as well as garden centers. But pop a note into your phone calendar now to remind yourself to plant hyacinth bulbs in September for bowls of fragrant Christmas flowers.

Once they bloom, keep your hyacinths in a cool spot to preserve the flowers for as long as possible. After flowering, you can replant bulbs outside in zones 4-8.

Recent findings suggest that cupressus macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’ is a variety of lemon cypress in a unique shade of yellow-green with a delicious citrus aroma. If you feel that holiday scents are sometimes a little too sweet and cloying, this is the plant you need to balance that with a fresh, clean perfume. As this evergreen is Christmas tree-shaped, lemon cypress adds a latest element to traditional holiday greenery too.

A great option for growing in a pot is the dwarf lemon cypress 'Wilma Goldcrest', available from trees.com. Though capable of eventually growing to 6 feet high and 1-2 feet wide, by growing this compact form in a planter, you can easily keep it small enough to bring indoors as a holiday houseplant for many years to come.

Position lemon cypress where the foliage will be brushed against as this is how the aroma is released, or you can simply crush the foliage between finger and thumb for a fresh burst of fragrance whenever you fancy. Your lemon cypress will need bright light but fairly cool temperatures. Water the pot regularly to avoid total dryness, but don’t let the roots sit in soggy soil. This compact tree grows best outdoors so move it outside after the holidays in zones 7-11, or overwinter indoors as a houseplant in zones 3-6.

It has been revealed that scented geraniums (Pelargonium spp.) offer the ultimate opportunity to customize your holiday fragrance profile. There are varieties with foliage that smells like roses, citrus, apple, ginger, cinnamon, chocolate mint and even nutmeg. Mix and match or pair with other houseplants to concoct a signature Christmas scent.

According to recent reports, at this time of the year, the best place to find plants is via the Etsy scented geranium live plants hub which lists available stock from verified independent nurseries. You’ll get the most out of your scented geraniums by placing them where you can rub the leaves to release a burst of fragrance. They need a sunny spot, too, as well as soil that drains well. Water when the soil begins to dry and pinch back stems to keep the foliage dense.

Scented geraniums can be grown outdoors year-round in zones 10-11, while in cooler climates they're best treated as winter houseplants that enjoy the summer outside on a sunny patio.

For a unique chocolatey aroma, Oncidium Heaven Scent 'Redolence' is an orchid with a wonderfully sweet chocolate fragrance. You’ll also enjoy the elegant spikes of burgundy and white flowers that last for a month or more. Look out, too, for Oncidium Aka Baby 'Raspberry Chocolate' with a lighter but no less lovely chocolate perfume.

It's best to buy speciality orchids from specialist nurseries, and to be sure you’ll have aromatic flowers for the holidays, buy a plant that is already in bud or bloom. Akatsuka Orchid Gardens is one such nursery, based in Hawaii and stocking both the Heaven Scent 'Redolence' orchid and 'Raspberry Chocolate' orchid in bud and bloom. These orchids grow best in bright but indirect light and in a potting mix designed specifically for orchids. Water when the mix is dry and avoid overwatering or letting the mix get soggy. Good air circulation is also a must, and keep orchids as houseplants year-round.

A few simple practices will keep your aromatic holiday houseplants fresh and fragrant:.

#33069. Tech Report: No Need to Throw Out That Old Potting Soil – These 6 Unfussy Plants Will Happily Grow in It

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1124 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: No Need to Throw Out That Old Potting Soil – These 6 Unfussy Plants Will Happily Grow in It

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste.
  • Over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away.
  • Some plants actually prefer leaner soil.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste. Don’t be too hasty. That mix could still have plenty of life left in it.

Over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away. Bulky materials, like peat moss and compost, break down over the summer, too. However, reusing potting soil is possible as long as the previous residents didn’t have diseases or serious pest infestations.

Some plants actually prefer leaner soil. Here, I describe six plants that are capable of thriving in old potting mix. I also provide some tips for refreshing the soil to give the new plants a little boost.

Nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) is a beautiful flowering plant that grows as an annual in most gardens. Many types trail or vine, making them ideal for containers. The brilliant flowers come in shades of red, yellow, and orange, like in these Jewel Blend nasturtium seeds from Seed Needs on Amazon, which also offers other beautiful color mixes. Both the flowers and leaves are edible. If you live in USDA zone 9 or warmer, you can grow nasturtiums as perennials.

In a recent development, nasturtiums are good candidates for recycled potting mix because they are unfussy, easy to grow, and generally thrive in poor soil. They are also easy to grow from seed. Sow seeds in your used potting mix next year when it’s warm enough. Place the container in a sunny spot and water when the top inch of soil dries.

Moss rose (Portulaca grandiflora) is another annual in most gardens. This low-growing succulent, native to South America, blooms in summer and fall with flowers that resemble small roses. You can find a lovely selection of moss rose seed varieties at Eden Brothers, with a choice of colors to brighten up your containers. Moss rose thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soil, making it ideal for containers. Plants need good drainage, so they can sometimes struggle in beds with heavy soil or poor drainage.

Recent findings suggest that grow your moss roses in reused potting mix enhanced with perlite, like this Riare organic perlite on Amazon, or something similar to boost drainage. Place them in a full-sun spot and let the soil dry out in between waterings. Avoid overfertilizing, which can lead to more leaves and fewer flowers.

Sedums (Sedum spp.) are reliable and popular perennials for garden beds, but they also grow well in containers. This is a large group of plants, many of which are succulents suited to dry, poor soil. Many gardeners love stonecrops like ‘Autumn Joy,’ which turn gorgeous shades of deep red in fall. You can buy Autumn Joy sedum from Nature Hills to enjoy its colorful late-season display. You can also choose from among low-growing and taller clump-forming sedums.

Sources indicate that the most important part of refreshing old soil for growing sedum is to add a material, like perlite, to improve drainage. Place your pots in a sunny location and water only when the soil dries. Avoid using too much, if any, fertilizer.

Hens and chicks (Sempervivum spp.) are diminutive succulents that grow in rosettes and have delightfully fleshy leaves that can be bluish-green, copper, gold, reddish, or even two-toned. You can enjoy a mix of varieties with this hens and chicks plant collection from Hirt's Gardens Store on Amazon. While hens and chicks flower, they are grown mostly for their attractive foliage. Hardy perennials in many growing regions, hens and chicks also make great container plants. They produce small offsets, the chicks, that can be repotted for propagation.

In a recent development, hens and chicks naturally grow in poor, rocky soil, so they should do well in your spent potting mix. Just be sure to add additional material to boost drainage. The best containers for hens and chicks are shallow and have adequate drainage holes, like this Deroma clay bowl planter from Target. Grow them in full sun or very light shade and water sparingly, letting the potting mix dry between waterings.

Calendula (Calendula officinalis), also known as pot marigold, is a short-lived perennial in zones 9 through 11, and an annual elsewhere. Though it is considered a flowering herb, many people grow calendula solely for its ornamental value. The flowers are daisy-like and usually bright orange or yellow, although they can also be red, white, or pink. You can pick up calendula seeds cheaply on Amazon, but Eden Brothers offers some gorgeous varieties, including the Pacific Beauty Mix and the Sunset Buff calendula pictured here.

A Mediterranean native, calendula appreciates warmth, sunlight, and well-draining soil. It won’t tolerate soggy soil. It can thrive in poor soil but benefits from a little refresh of old potting mix with compost. Water your potted calendula regularly, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Deadhead the flowers throughout the season to encourage additional blooms.

Like calendula, cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus) are mostly grown as annuals and are only hardy in zones 9 and higher. Cosmos are easy to grow from seed and reward you with feathery foliage and delicate flowers in shades of red, pink, white, yellow, and orange. Burpee sells a wide variety of cosmos seeds, including the beautiful ‘Sensation Mix’ pictured here. They make great cut flowers.

It has been revealed that while cosmos tolerate poor soil, it’s best to refresh the old potting mix a little. Then, you can sow seeds and place the pot in a location with full sun. Use a large container, as cosmos can grow quite tall. Water the seeds and seedlings regularly to keep the soil moist, and then only sparingly.

In a recent development, while all of these, and many other plants, tolerate leaner soil, all plants will appreciate a little refresh of old, tired soil. A few simple steps will give you better results over the course of the growing season:.

Remember that not all old soil should be used. Disease and pests can be passed on, so don’t take the risk. Also, if you’re growing plants that aren’t as tough as those listed here, it’s best to start over with fresh potting mix. You should also replace the mix if it has broken down so much that it becomes muddy and dense when wet.

Sources indicate that remember, old potting soil doesn’t necessarily belong in the trash. With a little refreshing and by choosing the right plants, you can recycle that old mix and use it for at least one more year.

Latest Update: Sarah Jessica Parker's Christmas Tree Trick Is Stunning – And All You Need Is Baby's Breath

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanks to her stint in The Family Stone, Sarah Jessica Parker's name has long been synonymous with the holidays for fans – and even more so now she's shared her Christmas tree trick with us all!
  • Recent findings suggest that yes, it is now possible to give your Christmas tree that Carrie Bradshaw stamp of approval!
  • This underrated flower has spent most of its life being a supporting actor to bigger and better roses, or a wispy filler flower tucked into grocery store bouquets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanks to her stint in The Family Stone, Sarah Jessica Parker's name has long been synonymous with the holidays for fans – and even more so now she's shared her Christmas tree trick with us all!

Recent findings suggest that yes, it is now possible to give your Christmas tree that Carrie Bradshaw stamp of approval! And, somewhat gloriously, SJP's approach to festive decor has the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, which means you don't need a celebrity-sized budget to recreate the look. In fact, all you really need is baby's breath.

This underrated flower has spent most of its life being a supporting actor to bigger and better roses, or a wispy filler flower tucked into grocery store bouquets. But when Kristin Davis posted an Instagram video of herself arranging flowers blindfolded (as one does), Sarah Jessica Parker left a surprising comment: “You can use babies breath in your Christmas tree.” Say what?

Now, Kristin Davis (who worked at a florist in college) wasn’t keen on using it for her own tree (very Charlotte-coded), but she did share a rule worth stealing: if you're going to do it, then always arrange flowers in odd numbers, like three or five.

For me, though, SJP’s comment about using baby’s breath in her Christmas tree has set my imagination alight! And with that in mind, I asked some experts how I could use them in my own holiday decoration this year.

The biggest risk when it comes to stealing Sarah Jessica Parker's idea is overdoing it. Roberta Sabbatini, founder of ItalianTouch Events, notes, “The main mistake is using too much. The beauty of baby’s breath is its lightness.” Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home puts it even better, saying, “One loose spiral is elegant. Three is a snowstorm, and the tree disappears behind it.”.

Sources indicate that remember that odd-number rule? CEO of Florals Memories Nadi Melam clips her baby’s breath into “clouds” and adds them in threes, noting, “Baby’s breath looks beautiful on trees because of negative space.” Translation: let the tree breathe!

Recent findings suggest that for a spiral, Brooks gathers five to seven stems, wires each bunch at the base, and tucks the ends deep into the branches. Sabbatini also skips pushing loose stems into the tree and instead secures each little bundle with florist wire or ribbon.

It has been revealed that fresh baby’s breath is a diva out of water. Brooks states fresh stems “wilt within a day or two indoors,” while dried versions keep their shape all season and can be packed away for next year. Melam agrees that dried is “far easier to work with.” If you do love fresh, just be sure to add it on Christmas Eve.

If you don't have time for the drying process, this Bexikou dried baby’s breath bouquet comes ready to use, and its short white stems are well suited to wiring into small, airy clusters for your tree.

Drying your own for a Sarah Jessica Parker-style tree is simple. Bundle five to seven stems with twine, hang them upside down in a dark, warm, well-ventilated room, and check after five days, as outlined in our guide to growing baby’s breath. If you’re short on time, ready-dried bunches work just as well.

On an artificial tree, Brooks adds fine floral wire around the branch wire, since the stems are too light to stay put when someone brushes past.

Sources indicate that warm white lights, clear glass ornaments, and velvet ribbon are baby’s breath’s best friends. Brooks adds pearl baubles and silver or soft gold ribbon to the list, but warns that rustic burlap and heavy red ornaments “fight it.” Treat baby’s breath as one of just two or three ideas on the tree, not the whole script.

Pair your baby’s breath with a strand of Northlight 100-count warm white LED mini lights, which stay cool to the touch and give the soft, candlelit glow that suits a delicate white filler.

Dried stems are brittle and, as Melam notes, highly flammable. Use cool LED lights and keep bunches away from hot bulbs and open flames. Baby’s breath is also mildly toxic to cats, so if pets are around, keep it to the upper two-thirds of the tree and sweep up anything that falls.

Baby’s breath is easy to grow, so sow seeds next spring, cut and dry the blooms in summer, and next December’s tree is sorted. Will your tree look like a Manhattan brownstone from a certain Sarah Jessica Parker-fronted TV series? Possibly, but only if you resist the urge to add a fourth bunch.

Her work has appeared in outlets including Bustle, The Everygirl, Hello Giggles, and Woman’s Day. She also writes about the latest gardening news and emerging trends, from pollinator-friendly planting to small-space edible gardens and sustainable outdoor living. When she’s not covering a viral moment, she’s cultivating her own love of gardening and bringing a storyteller’s eye to all things green and growing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.
  • Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable.
  • It has been revealed that “This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” said FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.

Recent findings suggest that “Mr. Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable. This verdict reinforces our message: there is nowhere to hide for those who commit fraud. We will find you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law,” remarked U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes for the District of Maryland. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office, along with our law-enforcement partners, remains committed to rooting out fraud and holding accountable those who exploit our vulnerable victims and who steal our taxpayer money.”.

It has been revealed that “This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” said FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul. “Patrick Britton-Harr will now face the consequences of his greed and brazen crimes. In addition to this healthcare fraud scheme, Britton-Harr was previously convicted for investment fraud in which the FBI uncovered a separate scheme where he defrauded private citizens. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will not rest until fraudsters like Mr. Britton Harr are brought to justice.”.

Industry observers note that according to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Patrick Britton-Harr, 42, of Annapolis, offered COVID-19 tests to nursing homes across the country in 2020 when these facilities were desperate for COVID-19 testing services. After specimens were collected from nursing home residents and other laboratories performed COVID-19 testing, Britton-Harr billed Medicare for separate, high-priced respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests purportedly conducted in a laboratory he owned in Arizona. Britton-Harr falsely claimed to Medicare that treating physicians ordered these extensive RPP tests, which screened for more than 30 respiratory pathogens. In reality, physicians never ordered the tests for their nursing home patients, and several physicians testified at trial they had never ordered an RPP test for any patient during the entirety of their medical careers.

Through his organization, Provista Health, Britton-Harr fraudulently billed Medicare $18.7 million for RPP testing purportedly performed in just six months, of which Medicare paid more than $7.2 million. Evidence at trial demonstrated how Britton-Harr exploited inexperienced employees, including a family member and high school and college aged interns, by directing them to bill Medicare for an RPP test every time a COVID-19 test was performed. Britton-Harr further directed the billing of RPP tests supposedly performed at his Arizona laboratory after he had already closed the laboratory, barred staff from working in the laboratory, and no longer had the equipment necessary to run RPP tests. Additional evidence at trial proved that Britton-Harr billed Medicare for RPP tests that were never performed, including billing for tests for nursing home residents who were already deceased.

Britton-Harr used the proceeds of his fraud scheme to fund a lavish lifestyle, purchasing, among other things, a $112,500 Porsche 911, and making $25,000 monthly mortgage payments on his Annapolis waterfront mansion.

The jury convicted Britton-Harr of five counts of health care fraud and one count of transactional money laundering. Britton-Harr faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison for each count. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled at a later date. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

HHS-OIG and FBI investigated the case.

In a recent development, trial Attorney Chris Wenger of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Ari Evans for the District of Maryland are prosecuting the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice revealed the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

Recent findings suggest that the Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, right now comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.

According to recent reports, “National defense information is classified to protect the American people from bad actors around the world who wish to do us harm,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The details alleged in this affidavit reflect the behavior of a government contractor who exempted himself from a federal law governing the protection of classified information. “Following a referral from the Agency, on Friday, October 23rd, the FBI arrested a contractor who provided services to CIA for alleged unauthorized disclosures of classified information,” remarked CIA Director John Ratcliffe. “The unauthorized release of classified material poses grave risks to our national security, intelligence sources, ongoing operations, and our officers. There is absolutely zero tolerance for leaking, and anyone who violates their oath will be held accountable and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”.

Those cleared to hold our Nation's secrets undertake a solemn obligation to protect that information. If proven at trial, this conduct is a grave violation of the Espionage Act, and the National Security Division will prosecute it as such.”.

Ian A. Brinksman, 42, of the District of Columbia was arrested following a search of his residence and charged by criminal complaint with unlawfully transmitting national defense information.

It has been revealed that according to the criminal complaint, beginning in 2020, the defendant worked as an employee of a U.S. government agency based in the Eastern District of Virginia and later in 2022 began working as a developer for systems integration for “Firm 1,” a contractor to the same U.S. government agency. During all times relevant to the complaint, Brinksman held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

A fundraising article reportedly published by Individual 1 in September 2026 claimed Individual 1 had “published reporting based on classified [relevant U.S. government agency] assessments.” Individual 1 posted on her social media profile, “I also accept leaks.”.

The FBI Chicago Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the Washington Field Office.

In a recent development, trial Attorneys Eli Ross and Kathryn DeMarco of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Vito Iaia for the Eastern District of Virginia are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Stuart Allen for the District of Columbia.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artem Stryzhak, 36, a Ukrainian national, was sentenced today to 70 months in prison for conspiracy to commit computer fraud in connection with a series of ransomware attacks that targeted hospitals, government entities, law firms, and other businesses around the world.

Recent findings suggest that “This sentence concludes a years-long, multi-continent investigation into a defendant who participated in cyber-attacks against Americans’ businesses and health care,” mentioned Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Cybercriminals who terrorize American businesses cannot evade justice by operating from abroad or hiding behind sophisticated technology. Artem Stryzhak’s sentence underscores the Justice Department’s resolve to dismantle ransomware groups, hold them accountable, and protect American businesses and people from cyber extortion.”.

Sources indicate that “Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors,” mentioned U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “Today’s sentence reflects that cybercriminals cannot hide from law enforcement and will face significant punishment for their criminal conduct. We remain determined to capture Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, a serial ransomware developer and Stryzhak’s co-conspirator.”.

“Disrupting a ransomware group that attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide and sentencing a defendant who had targeted healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic is of significant importance to this office,” said U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe for the Middle District of Florida. “We are proud of our law enforcement partners for their skilled investigative work in bringing this criminal to justice.”.

According to recent reports, “Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals,” stated Operations Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Branch. “These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses. Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners. Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.”.

Sources indicate that according to court documents, Stryzhak, formerly of Barcelona, Spain, conspired with others to perpetrate ransomware attacks on behalf of multiple ransomware groups against victim computer networks in the United States and other countries. The conspiracies caused significant damage to victim computer systems. Beginning in approximately June 2021, Stryzhak joined the ongoing Nefilim conspiracy as a Nefilim ransomware affiliate. Stryzhak was given access to the Nefilim ransomware and agreed with one of the Nefilim ransomware group administrators, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, to pay the Nefilim administrators, including Tymoshchuk, 20% of the ransom proceeds extorted from victims in exchange for Stryzhak’s access to the Nefilim ransomware.

The ransomware attacks that Stryzhak conducted with Nefilim ransomware included a June 2021 attack in which Stryzhak stole data from a organization in the oil and gas transportation industry. About a week later, Stryzhak created email addresses that were incorporated in a ransom note sent to the victim company. Stryzhak conspired with the Nefilim ransomware actors until at least October 2021. If a victim paid the ransom demand, the perpetrators provided the decryption key, enabling the victim to decrypt files locked by the ransomware.

Also according to court documents, Stryzhak separately joined the Hive ransomware group as one of its earliest affiliates. From June 2021 to January 2023, Hive conspirators attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide, including government entities, hospitals, and businesses. Hive ransomware attacks caused major disruptions in victim daily operations around the world and affected responses to the COVID-19 pandemic. In one case, a hospital attacked by the Hive ransomware group had to forgo digital technology to treat existing patients and was unable to accept latest patients immediately following the attack.

In his role as a Hive affiliate, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators deployed Hive ransomware against seven victims, including law firms, a dentist office, and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic. Victims were unable to access their encrypted data. The FBI, as part of a months-long disruption campaign against the Hive ransomware group, provided a decryption key to one of Stryzhak’s victims, thereby allowing that victim to decrypt its encrypted data without having to pay a ransom.

Stryzhak was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the United States in April 2025. Stryzhak pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud, extortion, and related activity in connection with computers.

The FBI Springfield Field Office investigated the Nefilim ransomware case and the FBI Tampa Field Office investigated the Hive ransomware case. The Criminal Division’s Office of International Affairs, the FBI’s New York Field Office, and Spanish law enforcement authorities provided substantial assistance locating, arresting, and extraditing Stryzhak.

Acting Assistant Deputy Chief James S. Yoon of the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), former CCIPS Senior Trial Attorney Brian Z. Mund, and Assistant United States Attorneys Alexander F. Mindlin and Ellen H. Sise of the Eastern District of Upcoming York’s National Security and Cybercrime Section prosecuted the Nefilim ransomware case. CCIPS Trial Attorneys Alison M. Zitron and Christen M. Gallagher and Assistant United States Attorney Hannah Watson of the Middle District of Florida prosecuted the Hive ransomware case.

The U.S. Department of State’s Transnational Organized Crime (TOC) Rewards Program has offered a reward of up to $11 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction or location of Stryzhak’s charged co-conspirator, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk. Anyone with information about Tymoshchuk should contact the FBI via phone at +1-917-242-1407, by email at TymoTips@fbi.gov, by contacting your local field office, if in the United States, or by contacting the nearest U.S. Embassy, if located overseas. More information about the Tymoshchuk TOC reward offer and one related to Hive ransomware is located on the State Department website.

In a recent development, CCIPS investigates and prosecutes cybercrime and intellectual property (IP) crime in coordination with domestic and international law enforcement agencies, often with assistance from the private sector. Since 2020, CCIPS has secured the conviction of over 180 cyber and IP criminals, and court orders for the return of over $350 million in victim funds.

It’s So Easy to Turn Your Garden Into An Owl Hangout – You Just Need 5 Plants

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1286 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there's something rather magical about spotting an owl in your backyard.
  • The secret is to think beyond the owls themselves (although there's never any harm in making an owl nest box) and create a garden that supports the wildlife they depend on.
  • Industry observers note that whether you want to lure in your birth month owl, or find yourself – much like Justin Bieber – welcoming in any owl that flits by, there are plenty of ways to make your backyard more appealing to these beautiful birds of prey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there's something rather magical about spotting an owl in your backyard. These mysterious nighttime visitors can be surprisingly elusive, but there are ways to make your garden a more welcoming place for them. And no, you don't need acres of woodland or a sprawling country estate to get your very own owl hangout started.

The secret is to think beyond the owls themselves (although there's never any harm in making an owl nest box) and create a garden that supports the wildlife they depend on.

Industry observers note that whether you want to lure in your birth month owl, or find yourself – much like Justin Bieber – welcoming in any owl that flits by, there are plenty of ways to make your backyard more appealing to these beautiful birds of prey. And the good news? Well, you can make a surprisingly significant difference with just five plants.

That's right, folks! If you want more owls in your garden, that means providing shelter for small mammals, encouraging insects and other prey, and offering trees and shrubs where owls can perch, roost or potentially nest.

From tall native grasses to berry-producing shrubs and evergreen trees, then, these are some of the best additions for creating an owl-friendly backyard.

Switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) is a fantastic native grass for an owl-friendly garden, particularly if you have a sunny spot where you can let it grow relatively undisturbed.

Recent findings suggest that why? Well, because its tall stems and dense clumps provide valuable cover for small mammals, including voles and mice, which are vital prey for many owl species. The grass also offers shelter for other wildlife through winter, when more exposed parts of the garden can become less hospitable.

According to recent reports, switchgrass is particularly useful in meadow-style plantings, where it can grow alongside native wildflowers. It produces attractive seedheads in late summer and fall, too, and it's a relatively low-maintenance perennial once established.

Give it a sunny position and well-drained soil, then, and leave some of its growth standing over winter rather than cutting everything back in fall. You may just find it swiftly becomes your upcoming favorite garden plant, let alone the best part of your owl hangout!

According to recent reports, if you want to make your garden more appealing to owls, don't underestimate the value of evergreen trees! Native pines and spruces provide year-round cover, with dense branches offering potential daytime roosting spots and sheltered perches. Their evergreen foliage can also make wildlife feel more protected from disturbance and exposure.

Different owl species have different preferences, but trees are an important part of the habitat for many woodland-dwellers like barred owls. Some species also use natural cavities in mature trees for nesting.

If you have room, consider something like this stunning Eastern White Pine from Nature Hills. Just remember that a newly planted sapling is unlikely to become an instant owl retreat, though, so it's always better to preserve mature trees where you can!

A slightly wild patch of blackberry brambles (Rubus spp.) might not be everyone's idea of a perfectly manicured garden, but it's a genius addition to anyone hoping to turn their yard into an owl hangout. After all, blackberry thickets provide dense cover for small critters and nesting birds, not to mention food and shelter for plenty others besides.

In a recent development, why does this matter for owls? Because a garden that supports a healthy range of small animals can help provide the prey that visiting owls need, of course! And you don't have to let blackberries take over your entire yard, either. A small patch of something like Baby Cakes® Blackberry Bush from Nature Hills along a boundary or at the back of a wildlife-friendly border can provide plenty of habitat value.

Just remember that brambles can spread, so give them room and keep growth away from paths and areas where people regularly walk.

Serviceberry (Amelanchier spp.) is a beautiful native shrub or small tree that brings several seasons of wildlife interest to the garden; think white flowers that attract pollinators, followed by edible berries in summer, which are enjoyed by birds and other wildlife.

Its value doesn't stop with the berries; serviceberry also supports insects and provides useful woody cover, helping to create a more diverse backyard habitat. For an owl-friendly garden, this is all about supporting the wider food web... but hey, it helps that it's a stunner, too!

Sources indicate that goldenrod (Solidago spp.) is often overlooked as a wildlife plant, but its bright yellow flowers provide an key late-season source of nectar and pollen for bees, butterflies and other insects. Those insects, in turn, help support other wildlife, including small birds and mammals.

It has been revealed that some smaller owl species also eat large insects, making insect-rich habitats like goldenrod a must for your owl hangout! Especially as it's a lovely way to add late-summer and fall color to your garden. Many varieties are native to North America, and once established, they're generally easy to grow.

Something like the Fireworks Solidago (Goldenrod) Plant from Burpee is a great way to go!

These five plants are a great starting point for your owl hangout, but there are plenty of other native choices that can help make your backyard more wildlife-friendly. #.

Recent findings suggest that viburnums, for example, produce berries that feed birds and other wildlife, while their dense branching offers useful cover, too. Native dogwoods offer flowers, berries and dense branching that can provide shelter for wildlife, not to mention some much-added beauty to any yard (there's a reason they're swiftly replacing magnolias for a lot of people!).

Industry observers note that junipers offer dense year-round cover and provide berry-like cones that are eaten by birds and small mammals. And purple coneflowers (Echinacea purpurea) attract pollinators and produce seedheads that feed birds and other critters, too.

Of course, planting is a brilliant starting point, but there are a few other things you can do to make your garden more appealing to these fascinating birds. As ever, try leaving some areas of longer grass and natural vegetation rather than tidying every corner. Keep mature trees where possible, particularly those with natural cavities, and consider whether a species-appropriate owl nest box might be suitable for your local area.

Industry observers note that it's also important to avoid rodent poisons, as owls can be exposed to rodenticides when they eat poisoned mice and rats. Keep lights to a minimum after the sun goes down, as they can confuse nocturnal birds and critters. And, finally, remember that owls need peace and quiet; take care to avoid disturbing potential roosting and nesting areas, particularly during breeding season.

Sources indicate that you might not spot an owl straight away, but by planting for wildlife and allowing your garden to become a little more natural, you'll be creating a much richer habitat for all sorts of visitors. And who knows? Before too long, your owl hangout might just be the most buzzing nightspot in town...

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend aims to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

Bringing Your Citrus Trees Indoors for Winter? Get These 6 Things Right to Avoid Leaf Drop and Pests

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A potted lemon or lime spends all summer on the patio soaking up sun.
  • Industry observers note that the move itself is a shock, though.
  • According to recent reports, that goes for a Meyer lemon, a key lime, an orange, or a little calamondin alike.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A potted lemon or lime spends all summer on the patio soaking up sun. Then the cold arrives. Citrus can't take a hard freeze, so in colder climates, potted trees have to come inside for winter.

Industry observers note that the move itself is a shock, though. Gardeners who try growing citrus indoors often find a scatter of leaves on the floor soon after. Indoor light is weaker, the air is drier, and pests that rode in on the branches can spread to nearby houseplants.

According to recent reports, that goes for a Meyer lemon, a key lime, an orange, or a little calamondin alike. Six checks before the tree comes through the door can head off much of that.

Recent findings suggest that most citrus can be damaged below 32°F (0°C), and a potted tree is more exposed than one in the ground. Lemons and limes are usually the most tender, while kumquats, satsumas, and calamondins can handle a little more chill. Aim to have the tree inside before nights start dipping into the 40s (4–9°C). Wait for the first freeze warning, and you'll be dragging a heavy pot from full sun straight indoors. Give it a week or two in a shady spot near the house first instead – it adjusts to lower light that way.

Flip the leaves over and look along the midvein. Brown soft scale (Coccus hesperidum) indicates up there as small, flat, tan bumps. Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) leave pale speckles and, eventually, fine webbing where the leaf meets the stem, and white, cottony clumps in the leaf joints usually mean citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri).

If you find anything, spray the tree outdoors with an insecticidal soap or a horticultural oil labeled for citrus, such as Monterey horticultural oil concentrate. Plan on more than one round. Once inside, keep it away from other houseplants for three or four weeks.

Sources indicate that bugs don't only ride in on the leaves. Tip the pot on its side, look in the drainage holes, and lift the saucer. Slugs, sowbugs, and earwigs all like that damp spot underneath, and ants sometimes leave small piles of potting mix they've hauled out. A slow soak with the hose drives many of them out.

Check any roots poking through the holes, too. Firm, light-colored roots are a good sign, but dark, mushy ones and a sour smell point to waterlogged soil. Unless the roots are in real trouble, wait to repot citrus trees until spring.

Recent findings suggest that citrus needs far more light than a pothos or snake plant. Indoors, aim for at least six hours of bright light a day. A south- or southwest-facing window is usually the best spot, with the tree close to the glass but not touching it. Up north, short winter days often fall short – that's when a grow light helps. Glowrium sells a dual-head LED grow light on Amazon that's just under 6 feet (1.8 m) tall, with heads that bend toward the canopy. Trees moved from full sun to a dim corner overnight often shed a good share of their leaves.

Sources indicate that hold a hand over a heating vent or radiator when the heat kicks on. That hot, dry air blows straight across the leaves of a nearby tree, and a cold, drafty window or door is no better. Sudden swings like those commonly trigger leaf drop. Somewhere around 65–75°F (18–24°C) by day and a little cooler at night, about 55–65°F (13–18°C), works well.

Humidity near 50% helps in a heated house. The Pure Enrichment MistAire humidifier from Walmart runs up to 25 hours on a tank, and the ThermoPro digital hygrometer can sit by the pot to track both.

On a hot patio, potted citrus can need water every day or two. Indoors, with cooler rooms and less light, it uses much less, and the summer routine can drown the roots. Push a finger about 2 inches (5 cm) into the mix, and water only when it feels dry at that depth. Deep pots are harder to judge, which is where a moisture meter, like the Xlux Long Probe Plant Soil Moisture Meter, is invaluable.

Water until some drains out, then empty the saucer. Set the pot on a few terra-cotta Pot Toes to keep the drainage holes clear. Don't overcorrect, though – a tree left bone dry for long stretches drops flowers and can lose leaves.

It has been revealed that some leaf drop in the first few weeks is common. Less light, drier air, and new temperatures all hit at once, and a few leaves on the floor are just part of it, mostly.

Look closer if leaves keep falling after the first month or whole branches go bare. A wet, sour-smelling mix points to overwatering, while a mix that's dry all the way down means it went too long between drinks. Check how close the tree sits to a vent or cold door, and whether that window is as bright in December as it seemed in October. Sticky spots, webbing, or cottony clumps under the leaves mean pests got past the quarantine.

Get through those six checks, and your tree has an easier winter ahead. Come spring, once nights stay above 50°F (10°C), it can head back out to the patio a little at a time.

According to recent reports, tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.
