#33062. How to Use Ornamental Edibles for Eye-Catching Containers

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2191 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finegardening ↗ Open Full Page

How to Use Ornamental Edibles for Eye-Catching Containers

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re looking past vegetables, fruits, and herbs because you think they only belong in the kitchen garden, you’re missing a whole range of interesting, versatile possibilities for creating exciting ornamental containers.
  • Sources indicate that as a designer, I create vignettes in my gardens that engage the senses.
  • Read More: Best Sensory Garden Plants for Sound, Touch, Taste & Smell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re looking past vegetables, fruits, and herbs because you think they only belong in the kitchen garden, you’re missing a whole range of interesting, versatile possibilities for creating exciting ornamental containers. Edible plants can bring striking foliage, flowers, fruit, and structure to a container, even when producing a harvest isn’t the primary goal.

Sources indicate that as a designer, I create vignettes in my gardens that engage the senses. It’s no different when composing a container or a grouping of containers. For now, set aside flavor and look at their other sensory qualities: visual appeal, fragrance, texture, and even the sounds of foliage and seed heads moving in the wind.

Read More: Best Sensory Garden Plants for Sound, Touch, Taste & Smell.

Successful container design balances aesthetics with the growing needs of individual plants. Before exploring specific edimentals—plants valued for both their edible and ornamental qualities—consider a few practical guidelines.

Growing vegetables in containers demands certain conditions if you want a good harvest. But when appearance takes priority over production, you can make different choices. For instance, allowing lettuce and other leafy greens to bolt can introduce interesting flower stalks and seed heads, even though the leaves may become bitter and less desirable for eating.

According to recent reports, containers give you greater control over growing conditions, but plants still need the right light, moisture, and soil. Choose edible varieties that tend to be compact, dwarf, bush, or well-behaved vines or climbers.

It’s helpful to choose the largest container your budget and space will allow. Larger pots generally provide more room for roots and retain moisture longer, while smaller containers dry out more swiftly and may require more frequent watering and feeding. Mixing container sizes also adds visual interest to a display. Whatever the size, make sure the container has adequate drainage.

Industry observers note that one advantage of container gardening is the ability to tailor the soil to your plants’ needs. Start with a quality potting mix and choose plants with similar preferences for drainage, moisture, and soil acidity. This flexibility also lets you grow plants that might struggle in your native garden soil.

In a recent development, because container plants depend on a limited volume of soil, they may need supplemental fertilizer as nutrients become depleted. Think about what you’re trying to encourage: Excess nitrogen, for example, can promote leafy growth at the expense of flowers or fruit. Choose a fertilizer appropriate for your plants, follow label directions, and consult your local nursery or Extension service for specific recommendations.

Sources indicate that mulch helps regulate soil temperature and retain moisture, even in containers. For open compositions where the soil surface is visible, use decorative materials such as small pine cones, shells, buckwheat hulls, or gravel. Leaf mold and finely shredded bark work well, too. Apply a shallow layer that allows water to pass through, and keep mulch away from plant crowns and stems.

Use what you have and think about growing your own. Many vegetables are quite easy to start from seed. Growing your own is both economical and a way to reduce the need for purchased transplants, especially when you use peat-free soil mixes. Choosing peat-free mixes can also help reduce demand for peat extracted from carbon-storing wetlands. Collect rainwater where permitted for an additional irrigation source. Avoid using untreated household gray water on edible crops. Incorporating perennials also extends the life of your displays. They can be combined with seasonal plants or relocated elsewhere in the garden when a container needs refreshing.

Recent findings suggest that the ever-popular Thriller-Filler-Spiller container method holds its ground because of its snappy moniker and reliable formula. In this method, the thriller is the dramatic focal point; the filler is a bushy, mid-level plant or plants; and the spiller—wait for it—spills over the edge of the container. It’s an easy enough recipe that most people can create something attractive, but truthfully, many fail to think much about what they are combining, which results in the massive-box special: a nondescript spiky grass towering over a showy fuchsia, with invasive creeping Jenny (Lysimachia nummularia, Zones 3–9) trailing out.

We can do better. While perhaps less catchy, think about composing your container much like you might a landscape. Consider structure (the framework); form and habit (the shape); spatial orientation (how it reads visually—does the plant have a horizontal, vertical, or some other orientation?); visual texture (is the foliage fine, coarse, or medium?); and color (is it intense, receding, or something else?). Go beyond appearance and consider the full range of sensory experience: how plants move in the wind and what that sounds like, what they smell like, and how they feel when brushed up against.

Industry observers note that not every plant or combination will hit all the notes, so don’t stress. Focus on a few complementary qualities. Combine the plants in your container to create contrasts or enhance similarities. Look at leaf, bloom, and seed head form. The idea is to create layers—low, mid, and upper—and aim for three to five plants that play off each other’s traits within the container.

Are you trying to create something formal, informal, transitional, organic, or eclectic? Knowing how you want your container to read to the viewer can help you make choices about which edible plants may be a better addition to the mix.

When composing your containers, don’t forget to look beyond edimentals. Often the best containers mix edible plants with purely ornamental plants, such as leafy or flowering perennials and small shrubs. The juxtaposition of disparate plants usually determines a container’s success—different textures, colors, heights, and forms.

In a recent development, while incorporating disparate elements creates visual interest, it’s also important to give the eye somewhere to rest. A collection of pots filled with different plant combinations can feel jarring without repetition or quieter areas to balance the display.

Recent findings suggest that A repeat may be exactly what it sounds like: using the same plant or using the same color, form, or texture across pots. Areas to pause are pots that may contain one uniform element—such as like plants, colors, or containers.

Industry observers note that another approach is to view the containers as individual components. Rather than composing containers with several different kinds of plants (including vegetables, of course), try grouping containers that each have one type of plant. This can be a powerful display akin to naturalistic block-style planting design.

According to recent reports, sometimes a container needs more. Perhaps it needs some staking for a vine, or simply a bit of additional texture. Incorporate natural materials such as pruned branches (dry or living), fallen branches covered in lichen, wild berry clusters, pine cones, grape or hop vines, dried elements such as grasses, or even small stumps.

And don’t neglect the value of seed heads—just because that kale bloom has now passed doesn’t necessarily mean you want to remove the plant; wait to see those prolific little yellow pods. And a radish gone to seed showcases its most redeeming feature: crunchy seed clusters that rattle in the wind!

In a recent development, by definition, a container is simply a receptacle for holding goods or objects, so feel free to think beyond the pots you find at the nursery. Salvaged and vintage items work well combined with more traditional terra-cotta pots. Take a high-low approach and use found items from your own home along with a special planter from a boutique garden center.

Don’t forget these irreverent options can also be repurposed in unexpected applications—that antique copper colander can go on to lead a latest life as a hanging basket. Just make sure repurposed containers provide adequate drainage and are suitable for growing food if you plan to harvest from them.

One of the biggest benefits of working with containers is the opportunity to modify them by adding or removing plants to capture the best seasonal foliage. While many edibles are annuals that end their season late in the year, others produce seed heads or even a second flush after cutback.

It has been revealed that some common edible members of the carrot family (Apiaceae), including carrots (Daucus carota, biennial); parsnips (Pastinaca sativa, biennial); parsley (Petroselinum crispum, biennial); and celery and celeriac (Apium graveolens, biennial), produce flowers in their second growing season. Their delicate foliage and umbrella-shaped flower clusters add texture and attract pollinators. Deep-rooted crops such as carrots and parsnips need sufficiently deep containers, particularly if you plan to leave them in place for a second season.

Osage orange (Maclura pomifera, Zones 4–9) isn’t a citrus fruit at all. This North American native tree produces large, greenish yellow, orange-like fruits with a distinctive, bumpy surface. Although the fruits aren’t considered edible, their unusual appearance and citrus-like fragrance make them wonderful decorative accessories for autumn container displays.

Another lesser-known edible is a well-known perennial: ostrich fern (Matteuccia struthiopteris, Zones 2–8). Its tightly coiled young fronds, known as fiddleheads, are harvested as a spring delicacy before unfurling into the familiar feathery foliage.

It has been revealed that lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina, Zones 3–8) offers similarly beautiful emerging fronds for ornamental containers, but it should not be treated as an interchangeable edible. Many ferns contain potentially harmful compounds, so accurate identification is essential. Only properly identified ostrich fern fiddleheads should be eaten, and they must be thoroughly cooked. For more information, see the University of Maine Cooperative Extension’s guide to fiddlehead safety. Of course, you can simply enjoy their fascinating emerging foliage up close in a container.

According to recent reports, vegetables that you may not have thought about embracing in your ornamental containers include okra (Abelmoschus esculentus, annual), with its large pods and hibiscus-like flowers; artichokes, such as ‘Purple Italian Globe’ (Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus ‘Purple Italian Globe’, Zones 7–10), with dramatic silvery foliage and purple flower heads (use your largest container); cucamelon (Melothria scabra, annual), also called mouse melon, which resembles a tiny watermelon on a prolific climbing vine; and leafy greens of all sorts. Look out for the striking edible red-veined dock (Rumex sanguineus, Zones 5–8), with the unpalatable common name, bloody dock—it’s a stunner. Its green leaves are marked with vivid red veins, and the young foliage is edible in moderation, although it contains oxalic acid.

More common edibles with uncommon traits include delicate currant tomatoes such as ‘Sweet Pea’ (Solanum pimpinellifolium ‘Sweet Pea’, annual) or compact tomatoes such as ‘Tiny Tim’ (Solanum lycopersicum ‘Tiny Tim’, annual).

Industry observers note that alpine strawberries (Fragaria vesca, Zones 4–9) come in a range of colors from white and pale yellow to pink and red, depending on the selection. These diminutive berries add character and spill over the edge of containers.

Recent findings suggest that peppers such as the teardrop ‘Biquinho Red’ (Capsicum chinense ‘Biquinho Red’, annual) are eye-catching and tolerant of many conditions. Compact blueberry (Vaccinium cvs., Zones 3–8) foliage glows red in the autumn, acting as a foil for its partners.

And there are so. Many. More. Whatever you’re interested in, you can find an edimental that will fill that niche.

Edible plants offer a broader palette that many gardeners and designers overlook—choosing them for containers broadens your range of plant materials and, most importantly, creates opportunities for delight and intrigue when used in unexpected ways.

Industry observers note that they also make it possible to garden in small spaces or places where in-ground planting isn’t practical. Containers can be moved to improve growing conditions, rearranged to create a new focal point, or grouped to screen an unwanted view. They also let you accommodate plants that might struggle in your native soil or spread too aggressively in garden beds, such as mint (Mentha cvs., Zones 3–9) or sunchokes (Helianthus tuberosus, Zones 3–9). Just be sure to give vigorous plants enough room to grow.

In the eastern United States, ornamental kales and cabbages, paired with mums, are a common sight this time of year. While there is nothing inherently wrong with them, now you know you have more edimental options, so why not experiment with a wider range of edible plants? From colorful leafy greens to fruiting vines and impressive seed heads, there’s no shortage of possibilities for creating containers that look as interesting as the plants themselves.

#33061. This Banana Bag Trick Triggers a Christmas Cactus to Bloom – Try it if You Don't See Buds By November

This Banana Bag Trick Triggers a Christmas Cactus to Bloom – Try it if You Don't See Buds By November

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if your Christmas cactus isn’t budding by mid November, don’t despair – this easy trick mimics methods professional growers use to force these plants into bud, and it's usually highly effective.
  • Pro growers require their plants to form plenty of buds at exactly the right time to ensure peak sales so, among other processes, Schlumbergera plants are often sprayed with synthetic hormones.
  • Recent findings suggest that we all know that leaving a ripening banana in a fruit bowl causes the rest of the fruit to rot, fast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if your Christmas cactus isn’t budding by mid November, don’t despair – this easy trick mimics methods professional growers use to force these plants into bud, and it's usually highly effective. It’s so disappointing when a Schlumbergera isn’t showing even the smallest pinpricks of colored buds on its stem ends by late fall, especially if you’ve been diligently delivering all the care your Christmas cactus needs in November. But by shifting your stubborn plant into survival mode, you can kickstart its bloom cycle. And guess what? All you need is a banana and a plastic bag.

Pro growers require their plants to form plenty of buds at exactly the right time to ensure peak sales so, among other processes, Schlumbergera plants are often sprayed with synthetic hormones. This causes the plants to stop growing green leaf segments and switch to developing flowerbuds. And you can use the exact same idea with the natural chemicals a ripe banana releases if your Christmas cactus isn't blooming yet.

Recent findings suggest that we all know that leaving a ripening banana in a fruit bowl causes the rest of the fruit to rot, fast. That’s down to the ethylene it emits, a natural hormone that plants release when nearing the end of their life cycle. So, by trapping ethylene around your Christmas cactus for a short time, you can trick the plant into thinking it’s under extreme threat, which triggers it to develop flowers as a last-ditch survival effort to preserve its genetics via seed production. Clever, huh?

Recent findings suggest that highly ripe bananas that have brown spots or are turning brown emit the highest levels of ethylene. You only need to use the peel: though the whole fruit produces ethylene gas, the soft, sweet flesh of a banana is a magnet for fruit flies and fungus gnats and adds too much moisture to the little greenhouse you’re about to create.

Excess moisture will quickly evaporate from the inner surface of the peel, further reducing humidity and any risk of pests or disease.

In a recent development, now stand your Christmas cactus, still in its container, on a plate or substantial plant saucer and lay the banana peel alongside the pot base. It’s important that the peel doesn’t touch the leaf segments or soil as this risks transferring mold or fungal spores.

Pull a clear plastic bag down over the plant, plate and banana peel, and tuck or tie under the plate to seal. If the bag is flimsy and falls onto the stems, use chopsticks or skewers poked into the soil to create a frame so there's no direction contact between plant and plastic.

It has been revealed that it’s important the bag is clear as an opaque bag is likely to take the stress a step too far and your plant may drop leaf segments instead of developing buds. It also means you can keep a close eye on your plant through the process. A clear unscented trash bag like this from Amazon is ideal as it's plenty big enough to make fashioning your mini-greenhouse easy.

Now your Christmas cactus is in its little greenhouse, it’ll quickly overheat if it’s hit by the sun’s rays so find it a spot in a bright room but out of direct sunlight.

The optimum amount of time to leave your Schlumbergera in its ethylene tank is exactly 2 days and 2 nights. This gives the gas plenty of time to chemically shock the plant and trigger bud development, without damaging the plant or giving mold a chance to develop in the restricted air circulation.

While professional growers use incredibly precise parts-per-million doses of synthetic chemicals, you can’t tell exactly how much ethylene your chosen banana is emitting. So, keep an eye on your Christmas cactus and if at any point the plant looks like it’s struggling or there’s the slightest sign of mold, remove the bag straight away. Don’t be tempted to leave the bag on any longer than 48 hours as too much ethylene can harm bud development.

According to recent reports, carefully take off the plastic bag, discard the peel and place your plant in the spot where you want it to flower, being sure to avoid these Christmas cactus disaster zones. After a week or so, you should see pinhead-sized bumps starting to form on the leaf segment tips and by two weeks, they should be clearly visible.

It’s vital you check your plant hasn’t already begun developing buds before trying this trick. Inspect leaf tips under a bright light – or use a cheap magnifying glass with LED light like this from Amazon – to look for any bumps beginning to form right on the tips of the leaf segments. These may be tiny so gently feel for them with a fingertip, too. If your Schlumbergera has pink or red flowers these little bumps will be bright but if your plant blooms white they may be green and harder to spot.

Industry observers note that if you’re in any doubt, wait a week and see if those bumps get any bigger. While using ethylene from ripe banana peel is a very effective way to get a Christmas cactus to flower, this hormone shock can also cause existing buds to stall if the process has already begun.

If this pro growers' trick doesn’t work, there’s likely an underlying reason why your Christmas cactus isn't flowering, that’s overriding the plant’s system.

According to recent reports, the banana bag trick is well worth trying if your Christmas cactus doesn’t have buds yet, and you still just have enough time to trigger your plant into producing flowers for the holidays. Next year, be sure to use the black-out hack that tricks your Christmas cactus into flowering right on time, and you won’t have to worry!

Meet The Christmas Tree That Flowers In Summer – This Stunning Evergreen Puts On A Spectacular Display

💡 Key Takeaways

  • And while it might not be the easiest Christmas tree for gardeners in the US to get their hands on, there are some beautiful alternatives that can bring a similar combination of colorful flowers and evergreen foliage to your own outdoor space...
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when you think of a Christmas tree, chances are you picture a familiar fir or spruce, perhaps decorated with twinkling lights and festive ornaments. But, for some people, Christmas looks a little different.

That's right; instead of bringing an evergreen indoors, many people celebrate the season beneath a spectacular flowering tree covered in brilliant red blooms. Meet the Latest Zealand Christmas Tree, also known as the pōhutukawa (Metrosideros excelsa). This extraordinary evergreen puts on one of the most eye-catching floral displays of summer, transforming coastlines and gardens with masses of vibrant crimson flowers.

And while it might not be the easiest Christmas tree for gardeners in the US to get their hands on, there are some beautiful alternatives that can bring a similar combination of colorful flowers and evergreen foliage to your own outdoor space...

Shop Flowering Christmas Trees:.

Native to New Zealand, the pōhutukawa has earned its festive nickname thanks to its spectacular flowering season, which coincides with Christmas in the Southern Hemisphere. Because, while much of the northern hemisphere is welcoming winter with bare branches and chilly temperatures, New Zealand is enjoying the height of summer... and that's when this remarkable tree really comes into its own.

Recent findings suggest that rather than having conventional petals, its unmistakable flowers look just like fluffy red brushes (which pollinators love). And, against the tree's glossy green leaves, the effect is nothing short of spectacular.

A post shared by Hahana (@hahana_official).

Although it can reach around 65 feet tall in its natural habitat, younger New Zealand Christmas trees can be grown from seed in large containers (although they need plenty of sunshine, well-drained soil and protection from frost).

It has been revealed that for US gardeners, growing one outdoors will generally be limited to warmer and frost-free USDA Zones, so it isn't necessarily a practical choice for everyone. Luckily, though, there are other flowering evergreens that can deliver a similarly spectacular effect...

Sources indicate that if it's the striking crimson display of the pōhutukawa that catches your eye, bottlebrush is perhaps the closest alternative when it comes to finding a flowering evergreen that might serve well as a Christmas tree. Especially as its bright red blooms have plenty in common with the Kiwi native.

Depending on the variety and climate, bottlebrush (available at Walmart) can flower from spring into summer, attracting hummingbirds and other pollinators to the garden. Many varieties are evergreen and container-friendly, too, although they prefer a sunny position and well-drained soil.

For gardeners who love the idea of a flowering Christmas tree, but prefer something with more traditional-looking blooms, southern magnolia is a beautiful option, as its enormous (and fabulously fragranced) flowers can measure up to 12 inches across.

Sources indicate that while it doesn't have the bright red flowers of the pōhutukawa, it shares some of its most appealing qualities: year-round evergreen foliage, a substantial tree-like presence and an impressive summer floral display. For smaller spaces, consider a compact cultivar such as this 'Little Gem' from Expert Gardener. It has a naturally narrower growth habit than many full-sized southern magnolias, making it a more manageable choice for smaller gardens.

It can also be grown in a large container so long as you treat it to sufficient room, good drainage and consistent moisture.

If fragrance is just as important as appearance, gardenia is another gorgeous Christmas tree alternative thanks to its deep-green foliage and exquisite white flowers.

In a recent development, oh sure, their blooms may be smaller than those of the southern magnolia, but they more than make up for it with their intoxicating perfume. And, as they don't naturally grow into large trees, standard-trained gardenias can make particularly attractive container garden options; generally best suited to warmer USDA growing zones, growing them in pots makes it easier to protect them from cold weather.

Something like the Frost Proof Gardenia from Nature Hills is happily able to handle temperatures down to 0-10°F, too!

The New Zealand Christmas Tree is a wonderful reminder that evergreens don't have to be all about foliage; indeed, some of the most spectacular trees and shrubs combine year-round greenery with extraordinary seasonal flowers.

Whether you choose the fiery red blooms of bottlebrush, the impressive flowers of southern magnolia or the beautiful fragrance of gardenia, there's no shortage of ways to bring that flowering-evergreen look into your own garden. And who knows? You might even find yourself looking at your Christmas tree traditions a little differently as a result...

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.
  • The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.
  • It has been revealed that this agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

It has been revealed that this agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution. While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

“This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”.

“HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”.

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Recent findings suggest that between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

Although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

Industry observers note that this case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.

Industry News: How to Spot a Houseplant With Spider Mites – and Prayer Plants are #1 Victims This Month

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that november is peak time for spider mite infestations in houseplants, and the symptoms can easily be mistaken for dust settling on leaves.
  • As soon as we start heating our homes in fall, warm, dry air creates optimum conditions for spider mites to thrive.
  • Industry observers note that spider mites feed on leaves and, left unchecked, can cause significant damage, and readily spread to other houseplants, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that november is peak time for spider mite infestations in houseplants, and the symptoms can easily be mistaken for dust settling on leaves. While spider mites can target any houseplant, prayer plants are the most commonly affected, with monstera and alocasia close behind. So, if you're disappointed to discover some houseplant leaves fading, looking dusty or appearing speckled with tiny spots at this time of year, don’t presume it's just dust: check to see if your houseplant has spider mites straight away.

As soon as we start heating our homes in fall, warm, dry air creates optimum conditions for spider mites to thrive. The time it takes for these pests to reproduce reduces as temperatures rise, and in cozy conditions a single spider mite can turn into a thousand in a couple of weeks. Which is why, when mid-November arrives, numbers suddenly explode and we start spotting spider-mite infestations in houseplants.

Industry observers note that spider mites feed on leaves and, left unchecked, can cause significant damage, and readily spread to other houseplants, too. These common houseplant pests can be easily managed, though, and the earlier you catch the problem, the easier it is to deal with. So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your houseplant with a spider mite infestation.

Recent findings suggest that first, rule out dust by wiping the houseplant's leaves with a soft, damp cloth. Then look for these signs that signal you could be dealing with a spider mite infestation:.

Spider mites are actually arachnids, like spiders, not mites. They are extremely small – about a half a millimeter – and generally gather on the undersides of leaves. Here they pierce the leaves and suck out the contents to feed. The resulting damage from these feeding spots are very small, pale dots on the tops of foliage that can’t be wiped away, and these speckled leaves are a tell-tale sign of an infestation. As the population of spider mites grows, you’ll start to see fine silk webbing, which can easily be mistaken for dusty houseplant leaves.

Houseplants with broad, thin leaves that are easy to pierce are the most favored. While prayer plants are the most commonly attacked, monstera, alocasia, ficus, croton, palms, English ivy and dracaena are also highly susceptible to these pests.

Industry observers note that early intervention is the key to success if you have a houseplant with a spider mite infestation. But, even if you're dealing with a heavy infestation, these steps will work, though you'll need to repeat them to break the spider mite lifecycle.

It has been revealed that it's vital to keep the affected plant away from other houseplants as spider mites can easily move from one plant to another. Move it to a different, plant-free room until the problem has been resolved. Now that you know what to look for, check all your other houseplants very carefully for early, subtle signs of an infestation.

It has been revealed that next, you want to get rid of as many of the mites as you can. The easiest way to do this is to place your houseplant in the shower or bathtub and give it a good rinse. Use a firm stream of water so the pressure rinses most of the pests off, but ensure the jet isn't so harsh that it damages the plant.

Recent findings suggest that be sure to direct the water to the undersides of leaves where the mites are feeding and at any webbing you can see. Follow the rinse with a thorough wiping with a damp cloth to remove any webbing still attached. This process is unlikely to remove all the mites or their eggs, so repeat the process every few days as fresh eggs hatch.

Recent findings suggest that regular rinsing reduces a spider mite population but it doesn't remove it entirely. To fully break the lifecycle, you'll need an insecticidal soap with a natural formula such as NatureStop Insecticidal Soap, available from Amazon, or a neem oil spray like Captain Jack's Need Oil Spray for Plants, also on Amazon. These organic options will treat indoor plant pests safely. Insecticidal soap kills mites on contact by breaking down their cell membranes, while neem oil disrupts feeding and reproduction and smothers pests.

In a recent development, follow the label instructions for whichever product you choose and be sure to cover all areas of the plant, including undersides of leaves and stems. This is notable as both products work by direct contact with the mites. Repeat the application as often as suggested on the label, as you’ll likely need several applications to get rid of pests completely.

Industry observers note that remove any badly damaged leaves, whether they're heavily stippled, have turned mostly yellow or have brown, crispy areas. Snip off with sharp pruners and dispose of them in the garbage (not the compost). Any foliage that's mostly green can be left and, while damaged leaves won’t return to their former glory, healthy areas will still photosynthesize and support the plant’s recovery.

Good houseplant care in fall will make conditions less favorable to spider mites:.

According to recent reports, if houseplant leaves have irregular patches of white or light gray powder on their surfaces that can be wiped away, this is likely a fungal infection, powdery mildew and should be treated by disposing of heavily affected leaves and using a product like neem oil or a commercial houseplant fungicide. A white film or larger spots could be mineral deposits from watering If you have hard water and mist or irrigate houseplants from above, easily fixed by cleaning leaves then avoiding getting foliage wet.

#33056. Industry News: Stop Wasting Time and Money on These 7 Fall Lawn Care Jobs – Here's What Your Grass Really Needs

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Stop Wasting Time and Money on These 7 Fall Lawn Care Jobs – Here's What Your Grass Really Needs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, fall is a time of transition in the garden, not just for perennials, shrubs, and trees, but also for your grass.
  • In a recent development, fall lawn care is all about working smarter, not harder.
  • This year, focus your fall lawn care on a few smart tasks that help prepare the soil and roots for winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fall is a time of transition in the garden, not just for perennials, shrubs, and trees, but also for your grass. Cool-season grasses perk up a little after the heat of midsummer, but now they’re getting ready for winter dormancy. Some of the tasks you might feel compelled to do now are unnecessary or even harmful.

In a recent development, fall lawn care is all about working smarter, not harder. More fertilizer, more water, and more cutting can do more harm than good this time of year. There is a persistent myth that more care is better, but the truth is that many homeowners do too much.

This year, focus your fall lawn care on a few smart tasks that help prepare the soil and roots for winter. Here is a list of typical chores you can skip this year and what to do instead. I promise, this will make your life a lot easier, and your lawn will thank you.

In a recent development, many homeowners love the look of a pristinely green fall lawn. Others think keeping it totally clear of fall leaves is critical to the turf's health. Keeping the lawn totally clear can be backbreaking work, and it’s not worth the effort.

It’s true that a dense layer of leaves, especially wet leaves, can harm the grass by trapping moisture and blocking sunlight. But some leaves left in place won’t smother the grass. Also, it’s unnecessary to physically remove every leaf.

It has been revealed that instead of endlessly raking, run a mulching mower, like this Greenworks model, over the grass as needed, chopping up the leaves when you see light to moderate coverage. Another option is to remove some of a thick layer of leaves for use in compost or as a mulch in beds. Don’t worry about removing every last leaf before winter.

Fall lawns typically need less supplemental water than summer lawns, so ditch your routine watering chore and play it by ear instead. Cooler fall temperatures reduce evaporation, so unless you have unusually dry conditions, you shouldn’t have to water lawns as often as in summer.

It has been revealed that A simple rain gauge, such as this easy-to-read JMBay model from Amazon, can help you keep track of rainfall. Keep an eye on the soil and rain and decide when the grass could use a deep drink rather than sticking with a strict schedule.

According to recent reports, of course, there are exceptions. If you have seeded parts of the lawn or installed new sod before winter, these areas should be watered regularly right up until the ground freezes.

In a recent development, at some point, there will be a final mow of the season, but blueprint to keep cutting regularly until the grass stops actively growing. Until then, don’t cut grass too short. Your turf needs substantial foliage to collect energy from the sun and build strong, deep roots. Cutting grass short leads to shorter roots, which struggle more through the winter than long roots.

Keep mowing to the recommended height for your type of grass until the final cut. A tool like the Oregon Deck Leveling Gauge from Amazon can help you check your mower's cutting height and ensure an even cut.

Industry observers note that as growth slows, you’ll need to cut less frequently. When it’s time to make the final cut, use the lower end of the recommended height range for the grass. It should be at a medium height for winter.

Bagging all of your healthy grass clippings is unnecessary. It’s also a highly labor-intensive chore. Don’t waste your time, energy, or back on this one. Finely chopped grass decomposes quickly and adds nutrients to the soil. And, contrary to popular belief, grass clippings left on the ground do not contribute to thatch buildup.

Sources indicate that instead of bagging cut grass, use a mulching mower. You might want to pick up some of the grass if you have a lot of heavy clumps sitting on the lawn, but most can be kept in place to decompose. The more frequently you mow, the fewer big clumps you'll get.

Recent findings suggest that managing weeds in the turf can be a useful fall chore, giving your grass a better chance of getting nutrients and water as it prepares for winter dormancy. However, it’s possible to overwork this chore. Many annual weeds will die as temperatures drop, so don’t bother with these.

It has been revealed that instead, focus your energy on managing tough perennial weeds. Examples include dandelions, plantain, and clover. Fall is a good time to tackle these with a selective post-emergent herbicide, such as Ortho WeedClear Lawn Weed Killer, provided the weeds are still actively growing and the product is suitable for your grass type. Alternatively, pull them by hand with a tool like Grampa's Weeder, which removes deep-rooted weeds without the need to bend down.

Fall fertilizing can benefit a lawn, but applying fertilizer automatically or getting the product or timing wrong can waste time and money, or even harm your grass. Warm-season grass is going dormant now, so feeding it can trigger growth that only gets damaged in cooler weather.

Industry observers note that cool-season grass is different. It’s gathering and storing nutrients in fall and also recovering from summer stress. Fertilizing now can be beneficial if the grass is still growing and the ground hasn't frozen, but be sure to use the right product. You can find fall-specific feeds at garden centers, often called winterizer fertilizers. One popular option is Scotts Turf Builder WinterGuard Fall Lawn Food, which helps lawns recover from summer stress and develop stronger roots ahead of winter.

In a recent development, your lawn doesn’t have to look perfectly green and manicured in fall to be healthy. Trying to remove every stick, branch, and leaf from the turf is wasted energy. It’s a thankless chore that won’t improve turf health. In fact, leaving some natural material in place benefits the local ecosystem. Next year’s pollinators could be hiding in the leaf litter or the hollowed stem of a fallen branch.

Instead of aiming for perfection, target your efforts at thinning thick mats of leaves, clearing walkways and drainage areas, and creating designated natural areas. Leave some corners of the garden undisturbed, where wildlife can shelter and survive the winter. Aim for a healthy lawn, not a sterile landscape.

According to recent reports, as you plan fall lawn chores, remember that type of grass matters. Know what kind of grass you have and what it needs in terms of fall fertilizer, weed protection, and mowing. All homeowners want to give their grass its best chance to come out healthy and green in the spring, but be smart about fall chores. Be selective about your efforts this time of year and focus on those tasks that will actually make a difference to the health of your lawn.

Breaking: November Is the Perfect Time to Plant These 6 Fruit Trees – You'll Enjoy Delicious Harvests for Years

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in France, gardeners and farmers have a saying that November 25 – the day Saint Catherine is celebrated – is the ideal day to plant a tree.
  • Growing fruit trees is a gift to yourself that keeps on giving.
  • Recent findings suggest that which fruit trees should top your list?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in France, gardeners and farmers have a saying that November 25 – the day Saint Catherine is celebrated – is the ideal day to plant a tree. ("À la Sainte-Catherine, tout bois prend racine.”) That may not apply literally to every tree species, but I can tell you this much: November is an excellent time to plant many kinds of fruit trees as long as the ground is not frozen.

Growing fruit trees is a gift to yourself that keeps on giving. Each tree in your home orchard can provide delicious homegrown harvests for years to come. Planting fruit trees in November offers many benefits. The cooler late-fall weather reduces transplanting stress, and seasonal rains keep the soil moist. That helps the trees establish roots before spring growth begins.

Recent findings suggest that which fruit trees should top your list? Many wonderful fruit trees are great to plant in November, so choose the one that grows your favorite fruit. But be sure to consider your local climate. Each fruit tree species has its own hardiness zone that indicates its cold tolerance. Some – like apples and pears – also have winter chilling requirements. You’ll also want to consider the mature size of the tree and be certain it will fit into your landscape.

Industry observers note that does life get any better than wandering out to the backyard and pulling a crisp apple right off your own tree and taking a bite? So when you consider planting a tree in November, don’t overlook apples. Apple trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 3–8, depending on the variety. You can plant either a bare-root apple tree or a container-grown tree in November, as long as the soil is not frozen, although spring planting is often safer in colder zones 3–4.

Sources indicate that there are many apple varieties to choose from. Most won’t fruit reliably on their own, so check their pollination requirements when you purchase your tree. Your tree may require a compatible cross-pollinator that flowers at the same time. For a great pairing, try a ‘Honeycrisp’ apple tree alongside a ‘Gala’ apple tree – both available from Trees.com – which can cross-pollinate and give you two delicious varieties to harvest. If you only have room for one tree, ‘Golden Delicious’ is partially self-fertile and can produce fruit without a partner, although you'll generally get a better crop with cross-pollination.

Plant your apple tree in a full sun location in well-draining soil. You may want to stake the tree to prevent any windrock until its roots anchor it well. You can buy a tree-staking kit from Amazon, but if your area is very windy, a crossbar attached to two posts will provide more support.

According to recent reports, pears feel like a fancier fruit than apples, but the trees are just as easy to grow and maintain. Like pear slices in your salad? With your own pear tree, you can pick sweet fruit anytime during the harvest season. Pear trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 3–10, depending on the variety.

Like apple trees, pear trees grow best in a full sun location in well-draining soil. As with most apple trees, pear trees are not usually self-pollinating. That means that you will need two compatible cultivars for reliable pollination and fruit set. However, there are exceptions. Both the ‘Bartlett’ pear tree and ‘Kieffer’ pear tree, available from Garden Goods Direct, are partially self-fertile, although they generally produce better crops with a suitable pollination partner. Kieffer also offers good resistance to fire blight, making it worth considering in areas where this disease is a concern.

November can be a good time to plant a bare-root pear tree in milder regions. The plant is dormant, but its root system can continue to grow during the winter as long as the soil remains sufficiently warm and unfrozen. It is also possible to plant container trees in November. Be sure the planting hole is several times as wide as the root system, but no deeper than the root ball.

If you want a tree with sweet, juicy fruit, consider planting a plum tree. The fruit is delicious when eaten fresh, but also makes great compotes or jams. Plum trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 4–9, depending on the variety. November is a good month to plant bare-root plum trees in milder regions, and it’s suitable for container-grown plum trees as well. Just don’t wait too long since you can't plant after the ground is frozen. In colder zones, spring planting is often safer.

Most fruit trees need sunny locations, and plum trees are not an exception. In fact, it’s particularly key to select a good site since plums flower very early in spring. If your tree is in a low-lying frost pocket, the blossoms will be vulnerable to late frosts. You should also pick a site that offers protection from harsh winds. Plant your plum in cool, well-draining soil. Wet, heavy soil can lead to root disease.

Most plum trees require a pollinator, so you’ll need to plant two compatible trees. However, several varieties are self-fertile, so a single tree is enough to produce a harvest. One great option is the ‘Methley’ plum tree, available from Trees.com, which produces sweet, juicy fruit without needing a pollination partner.

Most of us know that a peach tree is a deciduous tree with juicy round fruits. Here’s a lesser-known fact: the same botanical species can grow fuzzy fruits, called peaches, or glossy-skinned fruits, called nectarines. Peach trees generally thrive in USDA hardiness zones 5–8, although this varies by variety. Peach trees, especially bare-root peach trees, can be successfully planted in November, as long as the ground is not frozen. In colder regions, however, spring planting is often safer.

Industry observers note that peach trees need sunny sites. Plant yours where it will get at least 6–8 hours a day of direct sun. This is essential to trigger flower buds and sweeten the fruit. The soil should be well-draining since standing water will rot the tree’s roots. If the tree is grafted, be sure to set the tree in the planting hole so that the graft union sits above the soil line.

Industry observers note that peach trees also need a specific amount of winter cold, chill hours, when temperatures fall within the range of approximately 32°F to 45°F (0°C to 7°C). Standard peach varieties need from 650 to 1,050 chill hours, although you can find low-chill types that need as few as 100 hours.

One great option for colder regions is the ‘Red Haven’ peach tree from Trees.com, a self-fertile variety that produces sweet, juicy peaches and needs around 800–900 chill hours. For warmer regions with mild winters, try ‘Tropic Snow,’ a low-chill variety that needs just 225 chill hours and produces deliciously sweet, white-fleshed peaches.

The American persimmon is among our most overlooked native fruit trees. This species does not get the spotlight given to apple, peach, or pear trees, yet it offers so much: edible fruit, wildlife habitat, and attractive fall foliage. The fruit is an key food source for wild birds and mammals, including raccoons, opossums, and foxes, and it remains available into early winter, when many other food sources have diminished.

Native to the eastern and southeastern United States, these trees are very cold-hardy, thriving in USDA hardiness zones 4–9. You can buy a common American persimmon tree from Plant Addicts to enjoy its fruit and seasonal interest in your own backyard. American persimmons typically have separate male and female trees, but some varieties are self-fertile and can produce fruit without a pollination partner. If you're growing a tree for its fruit, check its pollination requirements before buying.

Recent findings suggest that the trees can grow to between 35 and 60 feet (10–18 m) tall, although they can be kept smaller by pruning. The fruit they produce is orange and initially astringent, but it becomes sweet and delicious when it fully ripens, often around the time of the first frost.

Recent findings suggest that november is a good time to plant an American persimmon tree in milder regions. You cannot plant at this time, however, if the ground is frozen. Find a well-drained area with loamy, organically rich soil in a full sun location. Avoid frost pockets since these trees may be damaged by unseasonable frosts.

Sources indicate that fig trees have a long and somewhat exotic history. They have been cultivated for 12,000 years and are among the earliest domesticated plants. They have deep symbolic meaning as symbols of peace and prosperity, but, perhaps more crucial to modern gardeners, the trees are tough, drought-tolerant, and resistant to pests and diseases.

Sources indicate that fig trees can thrive in USDA hardiness zones 6–11, depending on the variety, although those in colder zones may need winter protection. For a reliable, sweet-fruited variety, try the ‘Brown Turkey’ fig from Nature Hills, which is well suited to milder regions. Gardeners in colder zones might prefer the ‘Chicago Hardy’ fig, also available from Nature Hills, which can withstand much lower winter temperatures with suitable protection. Both varieties are self-fruitful, so you only need one tree to enjoy a harvest.

Recent findings suggest that if you live in USDA zone 8 or above, it is generally appropriate to plant your tree in November, provided the ground isn't frozen. In cooler zones, you should wait until spring. For November planting, select a full-sun location, ideally against a south- or southwest-facing wall. This helps the tree capture and retain warmth. The soil must be well-draining and slightly acidic. Water the tree deeply right after planting to settle the soil around the roots.

Once the tree is planted, apply a layer of organic mulch around the base, keeping the mulch a few inches away from the actual trunk to prevent rot.

In a recent development, robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse are fast becoming the it couple of the moment (not least of all because the man formerly known as Edward Cullen is now Bond, James Bond). So you'd best believe they're setting trends left, right, and center – even in the world of indoor gardening.

And while we'd expect the pair to have a suitably impressive garden, it turns out their houseplant of choice is considerably more interesting than your average monstera or spider plant. In fact, it's a miniature tree with a rather sophisticated reputation: the not-so-humble bonsai!

Sources indicate that yes, with the couple's busy schedules taking them between different homes and locations, it makes sense that they're all about the idea of bringing greenery indoors. After all, houseplants offer a lovely way to make a space feel personal, even when you're not necessarily putting down roots for the long term. And if you're going to invest in an indoor plant, then why not make it something a little more unusual?

Speaking to the Perfectly Imperfect Newsletter in September 2024, Suki Waterhouse revealed that she developed a rather unexpected obsession with bonsai trees during the final month of her pregnancy.

'When I was preggers in the last month and didn’t really feel like seeing anyone, I got obsessed with getting a bonsai tree,' she indicates. 'I found a number on Google and pulled up to a house in East Hollywood and a lady had a bunch of them locked up in her back garden. Felt super cool and mysterious. Some of them she’d had for 30 years. Fell in love with this guy and have become obsessed with pruning.'.

The leaves on this bonsai fold up at night or in subdued light, and it wakes up when we do!

It's a wonderfully specific plant obsession, and one we can absolutely get behind. Especially as there's something rather magical about a tiny tree that's been carefully cultivated for decade; there's a reason that bonsai is as much an art form as it is a gardening hobby.

According to recent reports, of course, Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson aren't the only ones who appreciate the appeal of the beautiful bonsai tree. In fact, there's been something of a growing appreciation for the slower, more mindful side of gardening, and bonsai? Why, that fits the philosophy rather beautifully.

More importantly? Well, despite the fact that bonsai trees have a reputation for being (whisper it) high-maintenance, they're not as intimidating as their appearance might suggest. The trick is choosing the right one – so look for a variety suited to indoor conditions and make a note of its basic requirements. And, as Suki herself pointed out, a little regular pruning and thoughtful watering can go a long way.

If Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson have inspired you to introduce a little bonsai magic into your own home, there are a few varieties worth considering...

If you're newly introduced to bonsai, ficus is arguably the best place to start. These tropical trees are considerably more forgiving than many traditional bonsai varieties and adapt well to indoor conditions. Their glossy leaves and interesting roots make them particularly striking, too.

Give something like this Small Ficus Live Bonsai Tree from Brussell's Bonsai a bright position with plenty of indirect light, keep it away from cold draughts and water when the top layer of compost begins to dry.

If Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson have got you in the mood for something a little more unusual, consider the Hawaiian umbrella tree (Schefflera arboricola).

This bonsai's distinctive leaves and naturally branching growth make it a particularly attractive choice for an indoor plant.

Recent findings suggest that it's also relatively tolerant of indoor humidity levels and can cope with slightly less-than-perfect light conditions, although a bright spot will always help it thrive. Take care to allow the soil to dry slightly between waterings, and prune regularly to maintain its shape.

A lovely option for anyone who tends to be a little forgetful with watering, jade bonsai (Crassula ovata) is a succulent that enjoys plenty of bright light and needs much less frequent watering than tropical bonsai varieties.

Pick up something like this Live Jade from Brussell's Bonsai, let the compost dry out thoroughly between waterings, and make sure it's planted in a free-draining bonsai mix to prevent its roots from sitting in excess moisture.

Recent findings suggest that of course, even the most beginner-friendly bonsai isn't quite a plant you can forget about. Even Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse will tell you, light, watering and occasional pruning are all crucial, and it's worth remembering that not every bonsai is suited to indoor living.

As a general rule of thumb, tropical and subtropical varieties are generally the best choice for growing inside; most traditional temperate trees need to experience the changing seasons outdoors.

Industry observers note that still, there's something rather lovely about the idea of tending to a little tree that could stay with you for decades. And if Suki Waterhouse's experience is anything to go by, it might just become your next very absorbing, very cool, very mysterious hobby.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The increasingly common term “eco-friendly” encourages us to think more carefully about the products and practices we use every day. When applied to hardscaping, it brings to mind materials and techniques that minimize environmental impacts and reduce our carbon footprints.

In a recent development, it’s exciting to have such a vast and diverse selection of landscape materials available for our designs and garden improvements, but many of those options have a significant impact on our planet through their creation, shipping, and installation. By thinking about how our hardscaping choices affect natural resources, pollution, and local ecosystems, we can create landscapes that are attractive, functional, and potentially more affordable.

In a recent development, with 30 years of experience as a landscape designer, I’ve recommended countless decks, patios, paths, fences, and other hardscaping elements to my clients, admittedly with minimal guidance about the actual materials used. In recent years, I’ve seen a notable uptick in clients who have expressed strong interest in locally sourced materials and in repurposing or recycling materials for these features.

In a recent development, some have even accumulated reclaimed bricks, large concrete pieces, and other materials with the intent of incorporating them into the design. This is exciting to me, as designs should balance the durability and longevity of products with a focus on resource efficiency and environmentally friendly options. These creative approaches are becoming more readily available and are being sought out by eco-savvy gardeners.

Read More: How Space and Structure Create a Living Oasis.

Conventional hardscape materials have a “production history” that often comes with a heavy environmental cost. This might include the lumber we purchase, edging materials, or the pavers and path materials we specify. Their history includes not only energy and resources used in production but also shipping and transport, and ultimately, their disposal or reuse at the end of their useful lives.

Recent findings suggest that finding lower-impact materials takes some research, but sustainability doesn’t have to come at the expense of durability or functionality. Interestingly, eco-friendly options can be more cost-effective over the long run because of lower maintenance needs and durability.

Sources indicate that hardscaping elements such as decks and fences are great examples to explore. Decades ago, the question for clients in my Midwest location was “cedar or treated pine” for most fences or decks. Now, the evolution and wider availability of composite decking and recycled plastic lumber have created increasingly popular alternatives.

Of course, the manufacture of composite lumber isn’t carbon neutral, and its environmental benefits depend on the materials and manufacturing processes involved. However, products incorporating recycled materials can reduce demand for virgin resources, and their durability may offer advantages over time.

Another option for traditional wood features is to seek out responsibly sourced, third-party-certified lumber, such as wood carrying Forest Stewardship Council (FSC) certification. This certification means the wood and products were harvested, processed, and tracked according to established environmental and sourcing standards.

Patios are another popular garden feature, and while I appreciate a nicely installed patio made with concrete, upcoming pavers, or bricks, there are some other options available. It is crucial to consider the permeability of our pavement selections as challenges of runoff and erosion come into play.

Permeable pavers, open-grid pavers, and some types of pervious concrete can allow water to pass through the surface and into underlying layers, helping reduce runoff when properly installed and maintained.

Repurposing brick or other paving materials from another project is also an opportunity to add a vintage look and possibly save money. I have a client who obtained more than 4,000 free vitrified clay pavers from the early 1900s (used for streets!) that we used for his paths and patios, and they look fabulous. Reusing these durable materials also kept them in circulation rather than requiring newly manufactured pavers.

Don’t neglect to check out the wide range of energy-efficient lighting options for your landscape as well.

Sources indicate that I’ve also been involved with some rustic patios made of upcycled concrete pieces that were fitted together like puzzle pieces, the gaps filled with plants. Research “urbanite” patios and paths, and see the amazing results!

In a recent development, it’s a great use of a common material that frequently ends up in our landfills. Crushed concrete is another useful material for paths. It can also be used as a base layer for paths and patios, provided it is suitable for the intended application. Again, local sourcing can reduce the carbon footprint associated with shipping and transportation.

Our reasons for supporting eco-friendly hardscaping decisions in our landscapes include, of course, preventing waste, conserving resources, and protecting our local and regional ecosystems and habitats.

While the convenience of buying readily available fresh materials may be appealing, taking the time to look into salvaged, recycled, locally sourced, and responsibly manufactured alternatives can yield equally attractive results.

Whether you’re planning a newly introduced patio, replacing an aging deck, or adding a garden path, find out what materials might already be available for reuse. Explore these opportunities!

  • Tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?”.

Perhaps he was hiding somewhere in the shade on that hot June day!

Sources indicate that earlier this week, I shared a look at the historic sunken garden connecting two homes built for sisters in Wilmette, Illinois. Today, we’re taking a look at another beautiful garden and a little Shakespearean history.

Tucked away on Northwestern University’s campus, the Shakespeare Garden has been around for more than a century! It all started in 1915, when the Garden Club of Evanston decided to create a garden to commemorate the 300th anniversary of Shakespeare’s death and celebrate the ties between England and America during World War I. They brought in renowned Danish-American landscape architect Jens Jensen to design the space, and by 1920, the club had completed planting a collection inspired by more than 50 plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s works. How neat! The garden was officially dedicated in 1930 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.

The Garden Club of Evanston still cares for the garden today, and it’s a wonderful little place to visit. Enjoy!

It has been revealed that while wandering the shady paths at the back of the garden, I came across this natural doorway formed by the trees. What a beautiful view of the central lawn and sundial! Jensen wanted the formal garden to feel like a clearing in the woods, and I think he achieved just that.

According to recent reports, the garden measures just 70 by 100 feet and is made up of eight planting beds originally arranged in a formal knot-garden design. (If you’re not familiar with knot gardens, look them up! They’re amazing!) In 1990, English garden designer John Brookes recommended removing some of the boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9) to make room for more perennials and a more relaxed planting style. He also had the sundial moved to the center to create a stronger focal point.

Industry observers note that the garden underwent a renovation in 2016 to restore several of its historic features, including the wooden obelisks seen here, stone benches, and pathways. The project also included replacing declining plants to help preserve the original design.

My favorite view of the garden! Formally informal.

In a recent development, jensen’s original planting list included everything from columbines (Aquilegia vulgaris, Zones 3–8) and violets (Viola spp., Zones 3–9) to poppies (Papaver somniferum, annual), peonies (Paeonia officinalis, Zones 4–8), and lavender (Lavandula angustifolia, Zones 5–8), all plants mentioned in Shakespeare’s writings. The plantings have changed over the years, but the garden still celebrates that connection.

It has been revealed that last, but certainly not least, this Elizabethan-style stone bench was installed in 1929, along with the garden’s memorial fountain. Nearly a century later, it’s still a beautiful spot to sit and enjoy the surroundings!

The Shakespeare Garden is open to the public, and I highly recommend stopping by if you’re ever in the area! You can learn more about its history and plan your visit through the Garden Club of Evanston’s website.

Recent findings suggest that I’m an owner-builder in Bay City, Oregon, in Marine Climate Zone 4C. I’m planning a single-slope roof with a 3:12 pitch and a 24-ft. clear span using parallel-chord trusses. My assembly plan consists of standing-seam aluminum roofing over purlins, 4 in. of continuous polyiso, taped Zip sheathing as the primary air barrier, and a truss cavity filled with 8 in. of mineral wool or fiberglass batts, for a target total insulation value of R-56. The interior will be acoustic fabric (a black muslin theater fabric) and then wood slats with gaps to form an acoustic ceiling. I’m not planning for an interior membrane planned so the acoustic function works as designed.

Industry observers note that my question is: With 4 in. of exterior polyiso and Zip sheathing serving as the primary air barrier, what building science function would an additional interior air or vapor-control layer serve? Would an acoustically open ceiling be compatible with this assembly, or am I missing a key risk? If so, do you have any ideas how I might make this work?

Sources indicate that thanks for all you do. I appreciate any guidance and absolutely LOVE the show!

One last thing: As a former radio host, I appreciate good voices, and Ian’s is so distinctive and awesome! It reminds me of Patrick Warburton, the actor who voices Officer Joe Swanson on Family Guy.

As a fellow Oregonian, I know the 4C climate zone well. In a lot of ways, its a Goldilocks zone—not too humid, not too dry. The climate tends to be pretty forgiving, with the exception of our frequent rains.

Sources indicate that as I evaluate assemblies, I always define and break out the control layers to see if there are any issues. Beyond water, air, vapor, and thermal, it is good to consider wind and fire control layers. The most glaring omission I see is a well-defined water control layer. I consider roofing to be a water-shedding layer, as water can get through via penetrations, mistakes, etc. You proposal to use polyiso, but you didn’t specify the facer type. In our area, the most commonly used facer in the roofing community is fiberglass faced, but aluminum facer is easily sourced, too. The former would make a terrible water control layer and the latter would be okay, except you would have to tape all the seams, and aluminum isn’t the most durable. I would start by installing a self-adhered WRB or roof underlayment directly on top of the polyiso. The permeability doesn’t really matter (more on that to come). This would be your primary bulk-water control layer. The next most important layer is the air control layer. As long as you tape the seams of the Zip sheathing, you should be good there. Pay attention to how  the roof air barrier connects to the wall air barrier to maintain continuity.

It has been revealed that for vapor control, of all the materials in this assembly, foil-faced polyiso would be the least permeable, as it is a Class 1 vapor barrier. If the polyiso is fiberglass-faced, it is a Class 3 semi-permeable vapor retarder, with a permeance of roughly 1 to 4 perms. The OSB in the Zip is roughly the same at 3 perms. In one sense, vapor control becomes less of a concern because you have created a vented assembly with the purlins below the metal roofing. In another sense, it may be a moot point because the thickness of the insulation should keep the Zip sheathing warm enough to prevent condensation. At approximately R-20, the exterior insulation would also meet the code requirement in our area. If vapor were to pass through, it would simply get whisked away via the vented gap. If you were to put a vapor-closed roof underlayment on top of the fiberglass-faced polyiso, the combination would essentially a layer similar to foil facing. In both cases, you are fine because the insulation is thick enough to keep condensation from forming on the bottom side of the Zip. If anything, a vapor-open membrane would be slightly more resilient, but we are splitting hairs in the weeds at this point.

Recent findings suggest that for the thermal control layer, the main change I would make is to switch to two layers of 2-in. polyiso boards in lieu of one 4-in. layer. Rigid insulation is prone to shrink, and by offsetting the seams you will avoid numerous thermal breaks throughout the assembly. On the interior, pick whichever fluffy insulation you like. Eight inches should work well, but adding a few more Rs wouldn’t hurt, either. From a wind-washing control perspective, mineral wool and wood fiber are denser than fiberglass, so I would consider those. One wants to avoid the thermal degradation from wind washing– think about a sweater on a windy day.

According to recent reports, patrick’s point about the fire control is valid. If you were to install a layer of Sheetrock and fire-tape it, its vapor-open nature means it wouldn’t affect the assembly at all. From a sound-control perspective, you might consider applying an elastomeric acoustic sealant and/or installing resilient channels before hanging the Sheetrock. From that point, adding the black muslin fabric and wood slats would work well.

I’m reaching out for some guidance. Earlier this summer during a storm, we lost a large tree in front of our house. It turns out that a good afternoon shade tree can cover up a few building science sins. In the 19 years we’ve lived here, we’ve gotten by with our AC air handler in the unconditioned attic. But without that tree blocking much of the afternoon and setting sun, the AC has clearly been working harder this summer, making it obvious that more than a newly introduced tree is needed.

I realize step one is getting a proper energy audit, but in the meantime I have a few questions:.

Sorry for the length of the letter, but I feel like this has all snowballed on me and could really use your help getting this project organized.

Industry observers note that thanks to Randy, Ian, and Cari for joining me and thanks to all of you for listening. Remember to send us your questions and suggestions to [email protected] and please like, comment, or review us no matter how you’re listening–it helps other folks find our podcast.

Tech Report: How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

💡 Key Takeaways
