  • I like to create purpose-driven designs.
  • Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that people often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a new house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

The same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

According to recent reports, in a latest garden, the major goal is often screening. Most people want privacy to live their lives outside without having to see a neighboring house, road, commercial area, or vacant lot.

According to recent reports, privacy was one of the big considerations when planning my grass garden. There was no privacy between my property and the neighboring property. I could see my neighbors eat their dinner, watch them play with their grandchildren, and even see them argue. Their house was also too close to the property line, and in fact, their sidewalk was on my property. That was a problem.

Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

I started out with some tall elements at the back of the bed to start the screening process. I positioned these plants so I could maintain them from my property without having branches extend over the property line. Keeping their mature size in mind also helped avoid potential conflicts with the neighboring property. Soft screens made of trees and tall shrubs (both evergreen and deciduous) offer privacy without creating a harsh, artificial boundary line.

Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options.

Looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

Understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

What a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden.

Growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from massive cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

According to recent reports, even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build upcoming nests.

According to recent reports, the ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

Susan Calhoun is the owner and principal designer of Plantswoman Design in Bainbridge Island, Washington.

Industry observers note that today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:.

Recent findings suggest that in Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

Arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

Sources indicate that absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

In a recent development, one of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

According to recent reports, there is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

In a recent development, just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

According to recent reports, another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

Tall conifers create a fantastic privacy screen in this view. The garden really is its own secluded paradise.

A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

Recent findings suggest that zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

According to recent reports, thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something fresh to admire.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

This is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

In the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

Sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy says she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what newly introduced plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

Hi GPOD! Yesterday we enjoyed some beautiful fall color in Nancy’s Massachusetts garden, and today we’re heading west to see what fall looked like in Colorado this year.

Industry observers note that bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie indicates the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:.

It has been revealed that colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

Welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

Other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

Sources indicate that I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

Another view from the front yard.

A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

Recent findings suggest that thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

In a recent development, welcome to the Fine Homebuilding Podcast, our weekly discussion of building, remodeling, and design topics aimed at anybody who cares deeply about the craft and science of working on houses. This is senior editor Patrick McCombe. I’m joined by Green Building Advisor editor Randy Williams, Fine Homebuilding contributing editor and operations manager for TDS Design/Build in Madison, Wisconsin, and producer Cari Delahanty.

Please email us your questions to [email protected]. You can find previous podcasts and check out the show notes at finehomebuilding.com/podcast.

Ian: House painting, interesting TDS projects.

Randy: Green Building Advisor updates.

Patrick: Upcoming article about surge protection by Chad McClung.

Grant referred to a house where he recently stayed as a “tiny house,” describing it as being about 16 ft. x 30 ft. I guess I have lived in a “tiny house” for 20 years! Ours is a Cape, built in 1953 by the people from whom we bought it. It has a 24-ft. x 26-ft. footprint and no dormer.

As discussed on the podcast, there are a lot of great things about a house this size. However, it is, in fact, too small. It is too small to comfortably fit furniture or closets or a family to gather to watch a movie. Our “primary bedroom” is 10 ft. x 11 ft. with a small closet out of that boundary.

It has been revealed that the full house could be arranged to be a very nice size for a couple, but it feels too small for four of us, especially with only one bathroom. I’m not sure how we’ve worked out the lack of closet space and single bathroom with three women plus me, but we have. When my daughters were in high school, I found it emotionally uncomfortable that most of their friends had bigger and nicer homes.

Putting my hurt ego aside, I feel they are lucky to be able to appreciate future living spaces that will likely be more luxurious than they are used to. My oldest daughter definitely had a better bedroom at college and easier access to a bathroom!

Discussion of Chris Briley’s recent low-voltage lighting article on Green Building Advisor.

It has been revealed that this article, “Low Voltage Lighting,” is from Chris’ Pretty Good House blog. Chris suggests that given the low energy consumption of LED lighting, do we still need line voltage lighting circuits anymore? Randy, can you briefly explain Chris’s premise? What do you think as an electrician? Does it make sense to switch our wiring methods for modern lighting? Ian, what do you think about this?

When you look at a finished house, what are the small details that make you feel the builder really took the time to do things right?

Recent findings suggest that I’m not talking about expensive finishes or high-end appliances. I’m thinking more about the little things that might not stand out in photos but make a difference once you actually live in the house—clean trim work, well-planned storage, good lighting, quiet doors, sensible outlets, properly finished transitions, etc.

I’ve noticed that some of the most enjoyable spaces aren’t necessarily the most expensive ones. They just seem to have fewer little annoyances because someone thought through how the space would actually be used.

According to recent reports, for those of you who have built or remodeled homes, what is one relatively small detail you’re especially glad you included? And is there anything you wish you’d thought about before construction was finished?

I’m curious whether the things people appreciate most are usually visible design choices or the less noticeable details behind the walls and throughout the house.

We talked about what gives you confidence in a builder, so now let’s talk about what you see most often on construction sites that is done poorly or incorrectly?

Thanks to Randy, Ian, and Cari for joining me and thanks to all of you for listening. Remember to send us your questions and suggestions to [email protected] and please like, comment, or review us no matter how you’re listening–it helps other folks find our podcast.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Sources indicate that A right-angle drill solves problems when a standard drill can’t reach—navigating between studs, working inside cabinets, or tackling tight corners. While this makes these specialized power tools handy in these situations, who truly needs a right-angle drill?

Industry observers note that plumbers, electricians, carpenters, and pretty much anyone involved in construction and renovation projects will appreciate having one handy. Even hobbyists and homeowners may need a right-angle drill when tackling certain jobs, such as installing cabinetry or assembling furniture.

Sources indicate that we test the top right-angle drills to find the best models for pros and homeowners. Our favorite was the Ridgid thanks to its comprehensive kit, durable build, and impressive power. Below, find the results of our hands-on tests and learn how these models earned their spot in this lineup of the best right-angle drills.

Recent findings suggest that any of the following right-angle drills will make it easier to drill holes and drive screws in tight areas, but each one comes with some pros and cons. We’ve detailed both the benefits and the downsides noted during our tests. Some models are best suited to light-duty use, while others are powerhouses designed with construction pros in mind. There’s sure to be one that will suit your project needs.

Ridgid’s cordless right-angle drill manages to be compact and lightweight while still offering  tremendous drilling and driving power.

Its head measures just 3.5 inches long, making it one of the shortest 18V or 20V angle drills we tested. Couple that with its slim profile and short length, and it fits easily into tight spaces inside cabinets and under-sink vanities.

Right-angle drills tend to be top-heavy, which can make them awkward to hold. With its compact size and light weight, the Ridgid was an exception. It felt comfortable and well balanced in the hand, which is significant given that these tools are often used in tight spaces where it’s not possible to get a two-handed grip. Adding to its maneuverability is a long trigger that’s easy to access from various hand positions. The trigger has ample rubberized grip, making it easy to keep a firm hold on the tool.

In a recent development, given its smaller size, we expected it to come up lacking in power. It didn’t. With a max speed of 1,900 RPM, the Ridgid had no trouble handling the larger bits we tested, easily boring holes with a 1/2-inch twist bit and 1-inch spade bit. It followed up that impressive performance by effortlessly driving ten 3-inch carpenter screws into a couple of stacked 2x4s. And if you need additional torque, you can get its max 375 in-lbs (inch-pounds) by dropping down to its lower speed setting.

What our tester says: “Ridgid’s right-angle drill is everything you want out of this kind of specialty power tool. It’s compact and lightweight while still packing plenty of power for drilling large holes and driving fasteners.”—Tony Carrick, Product Reviews tester and writer.

Get the Ridgid right-angle drill at The Home Depot.

In a recent development, ryobi’s tools have steadily grown more powerful over the years, slowly closing the gap with premium brands, and the PSBRA02 right-angled drill is a great example of the brand’s progression. With a max speed of 1,700 RPM and 350 in-lbs of torque, it can handle just about any job that requires this type of tool. Those specs also put it in the same ballpark as other cordless drills, all at a friendlier price point for DIYers who may not need premium performance.

Industry observers note that it produced enough power for drilling ½-inch holes with a twist bit and 1-inch holes with a paddle bit. It also didn’t struggle to drive a 3-inch carpentry screw through two 2x4s. The PSBRA02 won’t win any speed tests, but unless you’re drilling dozens of holes or driving loads of screws, you likely won’t notice the time difference.

Recent findings suggest that the PSBRA02 isn’t the most compact right-angle drill out there, nor is it the largest. Nonetheless, it fits into compact spaces thanks to a head that measures just 3.5 inches long. It also feels comfortable in the hand with a manageable weight, plenty of rubberized grip around the handle, and a long trigger accessible from various hand positions.

Get the Ryobi right-angle drill at Amazon or The Home Depot.

Looking for a 12-volt right-angle drill that delivers impressive power? The Milwaukee cordless drill caught our attention for all the right reasons. We tested the kit version of this small right-angle drill, complete with a battery and charger. However, users who already own 12V Milwaukee tools can order the drill as a “tool only” and utilize existing batteries.

This drill sits on the smaller side of the spectrum, weighing in at a mere 2.03 pounds. It slipped effortlessly into tight spots during tests, and its lightweight design let us comfortably operate it with just one hand. Since this drill packs less power than some other models we tested, it isn’t well-suited for heavy construction work. Instead, it excels at light-duty tasks like furniture assembly and drilling small holes in confined spaces. The integrated LED light was handy, though we did use an additional work light in darker areas.

Industry observers note that the real surprise here is the inclusion of a clutch, an essential feature that prevents stripping screw heads. What’s more, the elongated trigger design allowed us to adjust our grip up or down on the tool handle (based on comfort level) and still easily pull the trigger. While this drill is not intended for heavy-duty tasks, it’s a good choice for electricians, HVAC technicians, and plumbers who require precise screw insertion or minor hole drilling in tight spaces.

Get the Milwaukee right-angle drill at Amazon (tool only), Ace Hardware (tool only), or The Home Depot (battery included).

Look no further than the Bosch 12V Flexiclick drill. This handy tool boasts high and low speeds alongside a variable-speed trigger, and it performed admirably in our hands-on tests.

Unlike other 12V models, the Bosch Flexiclick isn’t confined solely to right-angle drilling. The array of attachments sets this drill apart, transforming it into a standard, offset, or right-angle drill by simply connecting the corresponding attachment.

One of our favorite features was the head’s ability to rotate in any direction. This allowed us to insert fasteners at any angle, though it required two hands when using the rotating head. Weighing only 1.2 pounds, this drill is comfortable for extended use, yet it offers an impressive 1,750 RPM—a remarkable feat for a 12-volt model. A magnetic bit holder adds convenience and also prevents the frustration of dropped screws.

For DIY enthusiasts and shoppers seeking versatility without the need for heavy torque, the Bosch Flexiclick is a game changer. We found it effortless to change attachments thanks to the one-click interface, and it offers the ability to use the drill in multiple ways. A convenient storage case keeps everything organized.

Get the Bosch right-angle drill at Amazon, Lowe’s, or Acme Tools.

Introducing the powerhouse of right-angle drills: The Makita DA4031. This electric drill stands out as a true performer. While it’s the only corded right-angle drill we tested, a host of impressive features make it an outstanding choice for construction pros.

Sources indicate that this heavy-duty drill features a potent 10-amp motor that provided unwavering power in our tests, drilling effortlessly through wall studs and joists. We found the second-hand handle indispensable for robust drilling tasks, as it let us grip it firmly while drilling for additional support. Perhaps best of all, both our right- and left-handed testers were able to use the drill comfortably, thanks to the ability to attach the handle to either side of the tool.

Industry observers note that the corded Makita made quick work of drilling large holes through ply materials and dimensional lumber. Its built-in clutch exhibited impeccable performance, effectively halting torque at low speeds when the tool met heavy resistance. With a drill this powerful, a good clutch is a must—not just to avoid stripping screw heads, but to keep you from breaking a wrist.

While the corded design offers a consistent power supply sans battery charging, it has limitations. Since we’re so used to cordless tools, we really noticed the Makita’s cord limitations, like having to drag a cord around and being limited to working near an electrical outlet.

For those seeking the ultimate right-angle drilling companion on the jobsite, it’s tough to beat the Makita DA4031 for its heavy-duty construction, durability, and reliable performance.

Get the Makita DA4031 right-angle drill at Amazon or Acme Tools.

In a recent development, deWalt’s 20V MAX right-angle cordless drill packs plenty of power, though this brawn comes at the cost of its maneuverability in confined spaces. Still, the DCD740 blazed through our drilling tests. With its high speed and torque output, it bored a clean hole with a ½-inch twist bit and chipped out a surprisingly smooth 1-inch hole with a paddle bit. It was also a fast driver, sinking 3-inch carpentry screws faster than other cordless right-angle drills we tested.

The DeWalt DCD740 has two speeds, so you can drop the speed down to max out the torque, which will help prevent stripping out screw heads. Along with its power output, the DCD740 also has a tougher feel than other right-angle drills with a metal chuck and thicker plastic housing.

The DCD740 is one of the brand’s earliest 20V cordless tools. It uses a brushed motor and is larger and heavier than other right-angle drills. Sources indicate that before testing the tools in this lineup, we researched more than 20 of the most popular right-angle drills and right-angle drill attachments. Our testing involved a range of tasks commonly encountered by professionals and DIY enthusiasts alike. We tested the drills’ capabilities in drilling holes through various materials, including studs and joists, to simulate the challenges faced during electrical and plumbing work. We also assessed their effectiveness for driving screws in tight spaces, such as cabinet bases and other confined areas.

In a recent development, throughout our testing, we paid close attention to the drills’ power, precision, and ease of use. We tested the drills with different types of bits—including standard, auger, hole-saw, and driver bits—to assess their versatility across various applications. We evaluated their power and performance to gauge their ability to handle different tasks efficiently. We also looked for ergonomic design and user-friendliness, considering factors like grip comfort and the convenience of features like LED lights and soft start-ups.

Finally, we awarded points based on a rubric: The better a tool performed a task, the more points it received. After testing, we averaged the points to help determine the best uses for the different tools.

The width of the head is perhaps the most crucial feature of a right-angle drill because it determines the space into which it can fit. However, there are several other key factors to take into account, including motor speed, power source, and weight. Ahead, learn more about these and other crucial attributes to think about when choosing the best right-angle drill.

Industry observers note that right-angle drills come in corded and cordless varieties, each with its own pros and cons. Cordless drills run on a rechargeable lithium-ion battery and offer the convenience and flexibility of not needing an electrical outlet or a cord. This lets you use them virtually anywhere.

Recent findings suggest that corded models, in comparison, require a standard electrical outlet. While these drills aren’t as convenient, a 120V power supply makes them more powerful while providing a reliable and constant power supply. Corded drills are also generally less expensive than cordless models. As with many power tools, spending more on a cordless model makes sense if it will see regular use. A less expensive corded model should suffice for DIYers who may use a right-angle drill only occasionally.

Size and weight determine a right-angle drill’s functionality and ease of use. Because a right-angle drill is meant to fit into tight spaces, size is crucial. Most right-angle drills have a head between 3 and 4 inches wide, so they can reach places standard corded and cordless power drills can’t.

Right-angle drills can also be short and lightweight enough to manage with one hand—although heavy-duty models typically come with a secondary handle.

Chuck size is also crucial. Most right-angle drills have a ⅜-inch chuck, which helps keep the head compact. Some larger models feature a ½-inch chuck for drilling larger holes or driving in bigger screws. These models typically have a wider head.

In a recent development, right-angle drills have ergonomically shaped handles with rubberized grips that let you hold them securely with one hand while drilling. Many also have detachable side handles that let you apply more leverage with the other hand. Some manufacturers equip right-angle drills with paddle-style triggers that run the length of the handle. This feature lets you better regulate trigger pressure to control the drill’s speed.

A drill’s speed determines how promptly the tool can drill holes or drive screws. It also gives an indication of how much torque the drill produces if the manufacturer does not provide that information. Speed is measured in RPM and, in most cases, is directly related to the power source. Most cordless 18V right-angle drills top out at around 1,500 RPM, while some 20V drills can reach about 2,000 RPM.

Corded right-angle drills have access to more power, which means they can produce more RPM. A corded 4-amp right-angle drill boasts around 2,400 RPM. While speed isn’t the same as torque, motors that can produce higher RPM are more powerful and thus capable of producing more torque.

It has been revealed that when assessing a cordless tool’s battery life, consider not only how long each charge lasts but also how long the battery itself will hold a charge before it needs replacing. Most batteries for right-angle cordless drills will last about 3 hours on a single charge with intermittent use and will take about 3 hours to recharge.

Recent findings suggest that lithium-ion batteries typically last about 3 years, or about 300 to 500 charging cycles, before they begin to lose their ability to hold a charge. This doesn’t mean the battery will stop working altogether. As a battery nears the end of its life, it will simply last for a shorter period of time and require more frequent charging.

As with standard drills, right-angle drills are capable of using various types of bits and attachments. These drills are adept at drilling holes with standard drill bits or driving in screws with Phillips-head, flat, star, and other styles of screw-driving bits. These drills can also use socket attachments to drive bolts. Like other power tools, right-angle drills use a variety of accessories, including drill bits, screwdriver bits, chuck keys, and other accessories that can be misplaced. For this reason, many right-angle drills include a storage bag that holds the tool, accessories, batteries, and chargers all in one place for easy storage and transport.

Right-angle drills also often offer convenient features like LED lights that illuminate the work area and switches that make it easier to control the drill speed, permitting the user to increase or decrease the speed range to maximize control and improve torque.

For more information on how and where to best use a right-angle drill, read on for answers to some common questions about these power tools.

A right-angle drill has a geared head that rotates the chuck 90 degrees from the body’s axis, letting it reach tight spaces and drill or drive at angles a conventional drill can’t.

This versatile tool is helpful for a wide range of projects. It can be invaluable for fitting into tight spaces when working on a vehicle. A right-angle drill is also ideal for drilling between floor joists or wall studs, which are spaces that are typically too narrow for a standard drill.

A ⅜-inch drill has a chuck that can accommodate drill bits up to ⅜ inch. Similarly, a ½-inch drill has a larger chuck that can handle drill bits with a maximum diameter of ½ inch. A ½-inch drill generally offers more power and torque, making it suitable for drilling larger holes and tackling tougher materials. It’s commonly used in construction and heavy-duty applications.

A right-angle drill attachment is an accessory that can be added to a standard drill or driver to enable drilling and driving in tight or confined spaces that are difficult to access with a regular tool.

It has been revealed that yes. A right-angle drill can handle drilling tasks that require high torque and speed, depending on the type of drill. A model drill such as the Makita DA4031 or DeWalt DCD740 can drill large holes through floor joists, wall studs, and framing plates with ease.

According to recent reports, most cordless drills don’t require you to do a lot to maintain them, but there are few things you can do to keep them in tip-top shape. Wipe off any sawdust or debris after each use, paying close attention to the chuck and air vents. Remove the battery when the drill isn’t in use and store it in a cool place. Lubricate the chuck periodically by applying a small amount of machine oil to the chuck jaws to prevent stiffness.

The biggest danger with a right-angle drill is sudden kickback that can cause wrist injuries. If possible use two hands when operating a right-angle drill, one to control the trigger and the other on the back of the head to stabilize its motion. If that isn’t possible, brace the drill body or your arm against a solid object, like a wall stud, to prevent the tool from spinning out if it jams.

  • Recent findings suggest that A wooden deck adds charm to a backyard and serves as the ultimate backdrop for outdoor relaxation, but keeping it in prime condition requires some work.
  • In a recent development, one of the biggest mistakes homeowners make when it comes to wooden deck care is pressure-washing it too aggressively, which often strips the wood fibers, splinters the wood, and leaves permanent marks, states Jon Colbasiuc, owner of Supreme Deck Store in Helmetta, Newly introduced Jersey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Recent findings suggest that A wooden deck adds charm to a backyard and serves as the ultimate backdrop for outdoor relaxation, but keeping it in prime condition requires some work. While weather certainly takes a toll, some habits you might practice unwittingly could be accelerating deck rot. We spoke to a couple of deck experts to identify common maintenance missteps, from aggressive pressure washing and harsh chemical cleaners to trapped moisture under potted plants and forgotten debris. By identifying these mistakes and adopting safer maintenance techniques, you can protect your deck from premature decay and preserve it for years to come.

In a recent development, one of the biggest mistakes homeowners make when it comes to wooden deck care is pressure-washing it too aggressively, which often strips the wood fibers, splinters the wood, and leaves permanent marks, states Jon Colbasiuc, owner of Supreme Deck Store in Helmetta, Newly introduced Jersey. When the wood splinters, it opens up recesses where mold can start to grow. This can eventually damage the wood grain, force dirt deeper into the wood’s surface, make it harder to keep the deck clean, and shorten the lifespan of the wood. Instead, Colbasiuc recommends using a soft-bristled brush with deck-specific cleaner, or pressure washing the deck from an adequate distance on a low-pressure water setting.

Another common concern is letting leaves, dirt, dust, pollen, and other debris build up between deck boards, which can trap moisture and eventually lead to mildew or rotting, notes Jake Anderson of Modernize It LLC in Candia, New Hampshire. It’s important to regularly sweep the deck with a stiff-bristle brush to keep it clear of such materials. “Regularly cleaning between the boards helps maintain adequate drainage and airflow, especially in the fall when leaves are a more prominent issue,” adds Colbasiuc.

Sources indicate that using a putty knife or special deck gap tool, clean the gaps between deck boards at least twice per season during spring and fall. Even covered decks can have debris that gathers in corners. Trim vegetation that’s within 12 inches of the deck to minimize leaves, berries, and other plant materials from falling onto the deck.

Featuring a telescoping handle and a narrow hook on one end, this tool allows you to clean between deck boards while standing.

Sources indicate that it might seem like a good idea to clean a deck with chlorine bleach, but you should avoid using bleach. The cleaner can be very corrosive, which will discolor the wood, and end up destroying the wood’s natural lignin, which can ruin its strength and structure. The bleach also raises the pH of the wood surface, which can make it harder for stains and sealants to work properly in the future. Finally, the bleach can ruin metal objects used on the deck, such as nails, screws, and fasteners. Instead, clean the deck using a nontoxic oxygenated cleaner with an oxalic acid-based wood brightener.

Industry observers note that another common mistake is leaving items out on the deck for long periods of time. “Rugs, planters, and other items sitting against the wood can trap moisture beneath them, which accelerates discoloration and deterioration of the wood,” warns Colbasiuc. This can lead to stains, moss growth, and deck rot. Instead, he recommends choosing breathable rugs specifically meant for outdoor use, elevating a plant container with planter feet, and moving the furniture every so often to help the wood dry between rains.

It has been revealed that you’ll also want to avoid doing anything that can scratch the surface of the wood. A common blunder is sliding around patio furniture with metal legs that can scrape the deck. Either lift the furniture when moving it or add protective pads. “Using metal shovels can scratch wood, create splinters, and scrape away at protective finishes,” says Colbasiuc. “Instead, use plastic-edged shovels, which are a safer option to clear snow from the deck.”.

Sources indicate that indoor air quality monitors can help you breathe easier at home by detecting hazards you can’t see or smell. Gases like radon and carbon monoxide are colorless and odorless but dangerous if inhaled, and these home devices may also identify other pollutants, including volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and airborne particulate matter like dust and pollen. They can serve as a first alert, signaling when to leave an area where the air is unsafe or prompting you to start clearing pollutants and head off health problems. Keep in mind, however, that not all air quality monitors detect all harmful pollutants.

Industry observers note that concerned about the dangers of hidden pollutants lingering in the air of typical homes, we decided to test a number of today’s most popular air quality monitors. We began by extensively researching more than 40 air quality monitors to narrow the field and then selected a range of models to test. (Spoiler: Not all of the air quality monitors we tested earned a spot on this lineup.).

Recent findings suggest that it’s easy to take steps to improve the air quality in your home with an air quality monitor. The best air quality monitor will depend on which pollutants you want to keep track of and whether you prefer a basic or tech-forward model. Our favorite is the Airthings 292 Wave Mini Indoor Air Quality Monitor. It monitors total VOCs (TVOCs), radon, temperature, humidity, mold risk, and outdoor pollen levels. It also comes with smart-home capability and easy-to-use air quality indicators, and it’s suitable for multi-room use.

Ahead, find out what the devices can do and see how the models listed below fared in our hands-on testing to help you choose the best air quality monitor for your home.

Bottom line: Choosing the right air quality monitor depends on specific needs, from detecting VOCs to integrating with smart-home systems.

When it comes to air quality monitors, accuracy is essential. While we didn’t have access to a laboratory for testing, we could offer a measure of control by testing all the monitors under similar situations to see if the readings would correspond when compared to one another. The following monitors all detected the presence of pollutants in our hands-on tests, and we would not hesitate to recommend any of them to help our readers choose a product to detect airborne pollutants in the home.

It has been revealed that to measure chemical pollutants in the air without spending a lot, consider the well-priced Wave Mini. The Wave Mini detects TVOCs, humidity, and temperature in the room. After spending a few hours exposed to a dish of oil-based stain in a closed box, the monitor’s TVOC levels spiked. When we compared its temperature and humidity readings to other monitors being tested, the readings were comparable. We believe it accurately portrayed all three readings.

According to recent reports, the Wave Mini offers visual indication of air quality in the room, which is accessible when the user waves a hand in front of the monitor. A light flashes green for “healthy,” yellow for “caution,” and red for “poor” air quality.

Sources indicate that users can purchase a hub separately, allowing them to integrate with smart-home products such as Google Assistant and Alexa. The Wave Mini also tracks outdoor pollen levels via the app that syncs with a local weather service. If users don’t have a specific need for monitoring carbon monoxide, radon, or dust, the Wave Mini may be just the right budget-friendly device to keep track of chemical pollutants in the home.

Get the Airthings 292 air quality monitor at Amazon.

Amazon, increasingly offering more of its own brand of products, has entered the air quality monitor field with this device, which measures particulate matter, TVOCs, carbon monoxide, humidity, and temperature. It’s ideal for bedrooms because the small white cube with a little stainless steel vent in front doesn’t have a large display that might keep some folks awake. Instead, a tiny indicator light at the top that shines green, yellow, or red notifies the user of the current air quality. We didn’t find the indicator light to be bright enough to be annoying; it was just bright enough to display the air quality at a glance. However, it only works in a darkened room—it’s not bright enough to see it in sunny daylight.

The Amazon smart air quality monitor syncs with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, and we found it simple to connect to both. We were unable, however, to connect the monitor to our Echo Show (not included), although it’s advertised as being able to do so. We’re not sure what caused the glitch, since our Echo Show and the monitor individually synced with the Alexa app, but it’s possible it will only connect with newer models of the Echo Show (ours is an older model). Still, the Alexa app on our smartphone provided excellent real-time readings and charts that made it easy to see the air quality.

We tested this monitor in our test box for VOCs and particulate matter. For the first test, we put a dish of oil-based stain in the box, gave it a couple of hours to infiltrate the air, and then checked the app. The VOC reading had spiked. We then opened the box to check the monitor—the indicator light shone red (hazardous air quality). For the second test, we shook the dust mop over the box and monitored the app on our phone. The PM2.5 reading spiked in about 5 minutes and fell 20 minutes later as the dust settled.

To test the CO sensor, we put the monitor in the garage, started the car, and closed the doors. We watched on our smartphone as the CO reading on the app rose. When we opened the garage door, the indicator light was red. We brought the monitor out into the fresh air, and the light turned green in about 10 minutes.

Compared with the other monitors we tested, the Amazon smart air quality monitor’s temperature and humidity readings were right on target. Overall, we liked this little monitor, and we felt it was accurate and discreet enough not to detract from bedroom or nursery decor.

Get the Amazon air quality monitor at Amazon.

It has been revealed that this monitor was quite an overachiever in our testing! It connects using Bluetooth technology via the Airthings app and provided detailed reports about our home’s air quality. It will also connect to smart-home devices, such as Alexa, but not via Wi-Fi. Instead, people must download the IFTTT app for their smartphone, which allows a connection between Wave Plus and Alexa.

The first test we performed on the Wave Plus was in a friend’s home where radon was previously detected and is being treated. They have a professional radon detector, so we wanted to see if the Wave Plus would also detect the gas. We positioned it in the basement of the home and left it there for a week.

It has been revealed that on our return, we checked the Airthings app and found a radon reading of 3.5pCi/L. This was the exact reading the professional radon detector was showing. When we waved a hand in front of the Wave Plus, it flashed a yellow light that told us the air quality was affected but not hazardous. When we took the Wave Plus outside in the fresh air, the radon level dropped, and the light turned green to indicate healthy air.

It has been revealed that we then tested the Wave Plus in our test box where we exposed it for 2 hours to a dish of oil-based stain, a product that contains VOCs. When we checked the monitor, the light was red (indicating hazardous air quality), and on the app we saw that the TVOC reading had spiked. We also compared the monitor’s temperature and humidity readings to those of the other monitors, which were consistent.

We performed one more test—a very unscientific CO2 test. We know that smoke contains CO2, so we took the Wave Plus to the garage and put it on a bench. We used our beehive smoker to blow little puffs of smoke directly on the monitor. The CO2 levels on the app increased slightly, and the indicator light turned yellow. We felt it was detecting some CO2, but we couldn’t tell if it was sensing as much as it should have been. Still, it registered an increase similar to the CO2 detectors on other monitors, so we felt the smoke from the beehive smoker didn’t contain much carbon dioxide.

The AirVisual Pro air quality monitor by IQAir boasts advanced laser technology, airflow control, and a crafted calibration algorithm to detect precise particulate matter and CO2 data. We felt the most vital readings on this monitor for allergy sufferers were the PM1, PM2.5, and PM10 readings. These sensors detect various-size airborne particles, ranging from pollen, which is rather large and can be detected by the PM10 sensor, all the way down to ultrafine dust that can’t be seen but is easily inhaled.

Industry observers note that the AirVisual Pro syncs with smart-home systems using either Wi-Fi or IFTTT. We tested both, and both worked well. After 30 minutes, the PM10 and PM2.5 readings dropped, as we suspected they would, because the dust had settled. However, the PM1 reading only declined slightly, which we think was due to the extra-tiny particulates that remained airborne longer. The PM1 reading didn’t drop for another hour.

The air quality monitor also detectsCO2 levels, temperature, and humidity. We tested the CO2 sensor by putting the monitor in the garage and blowing puffs of smoke on it from our beehive smoker. The CO2 readings increased slightly, but they didn’t spike. Still, that was consistent with our other monitor tests for CO2.

It has been revealed that this specific monitor had some trouble with temperature and humidity, as both readings were off by more than 7 degrees Fahrenheit/points compared to the other monitors. Sources indicate that those looking for a portable air quality monitor to detect pollen and other airborne particulate matter may find the Temtop P600 air quality monitor to be just the ticket. This monitor doesn’t sync with smart devices, so we couldn’t monitor the readings remotely from a smartphone. Instead, we checked it every few minutes to see if it had changed. The readings predictably spiked after 10 minutes and then gradually dropped (after about 25 minutes) as the dust settled.

Before we chose monitors for hands-on testing, we researched more than 40 models, looking for various sensor types and paying close attention to buyers’ reviews and ratings. We also reached out to an industry expert to get some additional insight. Lisa Townley, the associate director of product management/replacement parts at Carrier, a global provider of HVAC solutions, indicates, “As people are focused on the health of their indoor environments more than ever before, it’s imperative that they take steps to improve their living and working spaces, including the air they breathe.” She goes on to say that knowing what’s in your air is crucial because you can “take steps to lower the likelihood of mold … better manage allergens and asthma triggers … and create conditions for improved sleep.” She adds that air monitors with advanced technology to detect finer particles down to 2.5 microns or smaller are particularly useful in the home. We took this expert advice into consideration when choosing which products to test.

Recent findings suggest that for our actual tests—and we must say right off the bat that these were not scientifically controlled trials—we created situations we felt mimicked (or exceeded) real-life air quality problems. To test whether monitors with particulate matter (PM) sensors worked, we put them in a large box and shook a very dirty dust mop over the top. We then monitored the PM readouts on smartphones (or manually) to see when or if they spiked and when they fell (as the dust settled).

Sources indicate that we used wood stain, which contains VOCs, including formaldehyde, to test the monitors with VOC sensors. We placed an open dish of oil-based wood stain in the test box and allowed the fumes to infiltrate the box for a couple of hours before checking the readings.

In a recent development, we got a little more creative when testing other sensors! We tested monitors with carbon dioxide (CO2) sensors by blowing puffs of smoke directly on the monitors using our beehive smoker. We tested for carbon monoxide (CO) by putting the monitors with CO detectors in a closed garage with a car running inside. We tested a single monitor to see if it would detect nitrogen dioxide (NO2) by starting a wood fire in the fireplace of our she shed and then closing the flue and monitoring the readout on our smartphone.

To see how well radon sensors worked, we tested them in the basement of a friend’s home, where we already knew radon was an concern.

Temperature and humidity were casually tested by comparing those numbers with other monitors and using the average of the readings (minus the highest and lowest, which we threw out) to determine consistency.

We looked for readout increases and decreases but didn’t compare actual numbers. The detection numbers varied from monitor to monitor from the start, and we felt that one monitor might receive more exposure to a pollutant than another, even though we tried to keep the exposure levels similar. If the readings more than doubled, we deemed it a “spike.”.

We also examined and analyzed how easy it was to sync the monitors with Bluetooth; Wi-Fi; or If This, Then That (IFTTT) capability.

Industry observers note that to arrive at our awards, we gave models points using a rubric—the better we felt the monitor performed during a test, the more points it received. At the end of testing, we added the points and used them to determine the best category for each monitor.

Recent findings suggest that the monitors we tested ranged from single-pollutant sensors, such as simple radon detectors, to multiple-pollutant detection models that tracked the e humidity levels and several toxic gases. In most cases, a consumer will want a monitor that detects the type of air pollution that puts their home and family at the most significant risk.

For example, consumers who live in a region with known radon problems will want to look for a radon detector or a carbon monoxide detector if they’re concerned about automobile exhaust fumes seeping in from an attached garage. In addition, the following factors are key considerations for consumers shopping for an air quality monitor.

Consumer-quality monitors are not as precise as laboratory detectors, but they’re typically good enough to alert household members that airborne particulates and toxic gases are present.

According to recent reports, monitors that detect dangerous gases, such as VOCs and carbon monoxide, feature electrochemical sensors that react to the presence of gaseous toxins in the air. In some monitors, these sensors must be manually calibrated, but many of the newer models are precalibrated.

Monitors designed to detect dust, allergens, and other airborne particulates do so by estimating the amount of particulate matter that passes in front of a laser. Though valuable, these measurements may not be exact for two main reasons: larger PM might not drift into the laser chamber, and the laser might overlook the tiniest PM.

Home air quality monitors can detect a range of pollutants and will generally detect one or more of the following. Some may detect additional contaminants, but these are the most common.

According to recent reports, while some air quality monitors are relatively straightforward, others are pretty high-tech. For example, some models are Wi-Fi capable, and others connect to smartphones and devices via Bluetooth capability or IFTTT technology. Such monitors come with apps that can be downloaded to a smartphone, and then the app walks users through the installation process.

According to recent reports, single-pollutant detectors, such as carbon monoxide detectors, are among the simplest to use because they often just plug into an outlet. If they detect the gas in question, they emit a high-pitched alarm. The best air quality monitor for any individual should be easy to use, depending on the person’s technical skill level. Consumers will want to avoid choosing a complex model with a huge learning curve that requires watching online videos for hours just to figure out how it operates.

In a recent development, most air quality monitors are relatively small devices, with a sensor unit and a screen that displays how much of the pollutant is right now in the air. Portable units, which fit in a tool belt, purse, or tool bag, are the smallest of all. These are well suited for testing the air on jobsites or in rental homes that don’t have stationary monitors.

In a recent development, many monitors have the ability to detect numerous problem gases and pollutants and are suitable for multiple spaces. Those who want air quality monitoring to integrate with smart-home technology—so it can display information on a phone or respond to voice commands—will want to look for a smart air quality monitor.

Some people prefer visual alerts rather than numbers or charts that can be challenging to decipher. Today’s monitors often provide color-coded lights that indicate air quality at a glance. Typically, a green light indicates good air quality, a yellow light signifies the air quality is less than optimal but not dangerous, and a red light is a warning that the air quality is poor.

Response time refers to how promptly an air quality monitor will sense the problem and alert the household. Higher-quality devices often have quicker response times because their sensors are more accurate. Response times will also vary depending on which pollutant the monitor is tracking.

It has been revealed that for example, some carbon monoxide monitors will sound an alarm after detecting a low level of gas over a few hours; however, if they detect a higher level, the monitor will sound the alarm after just a few minutes. Monitors that measure dust and pollen may not emit a warning at all but simply track and record the varying levels of the pollutants by the hour.

In a recent development, air quality monitors are either corded (running on electricity from a standard household outlet) or battery-operated (powered by rechargeable batteries). Both are efficient, but for those who need to test air quality in a storage shed or another remote location, a battery-operated model is the handiest.

Sources indicate that very few things are as crucial as the quality of the air your family is breathing. If you’re newly introduced to air quality monitors, you likely have some questions.

According to recent reports, according to SmartAir, a developer of air filtration products, the accuracy of air quality readings on monitors falls between 70 percent and 85 percent. While most monitors are as accurate as possible, no single model is 100 percent accurate.

It has been revealed that the most common pollutants are airborne particulate matter, such as dust, pet dander, and pollen. However, some other airborne irritants to be aware of are carbon monoxide, lead, radon, and carbon dioxide.

Recent findings suggest that they sense high or unhealthy levels of particulate matter or toxic gases and alert residents if the levels become dangerous. Many options on the market rely on color-coded air quality indicators to alert people as to the status of the air quality.

Sources indicate that most consumer models can’t detect mold. However, consumers can purchase a home mold test with a petri dish and ingredients that will trigger mold growth if the home has a mold problem. While growing mold may seem counterproductive, it allows consumers to discover whether mold spores are present in the air, so they can take steps to locate the source of the mold and get rid of it.

Sources indicate that A fireplace should be a source of warmth, comfort, and connection in your home, not a source of worry, says Chris Maxson, owner and CEO of Acucraft Fireplaces in Massive Lake, Minnesota. But it takes some effort and upkeep to ensure your family and home stay safe. If your fireplace hasn’t been cleaned or professionally inspected in years, don’t light a fire until you’ve had it evaluated.

Industry observers note that “Just because a fireplace looks fine on the outside doesn’t mean it’s safe to operate,” warns Maxson. Even when a fireplace sits unused, the chimney can develop obstructions from animal nests, leaves, and other debris. In addition, moisture intrusion, deterioration, and damaged components can create potential safety concerns. Whether you have a traditional wood-burning fireplace or a modern gas fireplace, you’ll want to understand how best to clean and maintain it.

Sources indicate that it’s not safe to use a fireplace that has been neglected for an extended period. In general, you should clean a wood-burning fireplace and the chimney once a year before you start using it. Likewise, gas fireplaces need cleaning once a year or as recommended by the manufacturer. Here are the reasons to clean fireplaces, according to Maxson:.

In a recent development, wood-burning fireplaces produce soot, ash, and creosote as wood burns. Creosote is highly combustible, and accumulated deposits can increase the risk of a chimney fire. Both gas and wood-burning fireplaces also rely on properly functioning venting systems to direct combustion byproducts away from occupied spaces. Obstructions or damaged venting can contribute to dangerous conditions, including carbon monoxide exposure inside homes.

In a recent development, A clean, properly maintained fireplace is more likely to operate as designed. On the other hand, excessive buildup, restricted airflow, and neglected components can interfere with ignition, combustion, and draft.

Cleaning a fireplace isn’t just about making it look good. It’s about making sure the entire system—including the components you can’t see—is functioning properly. Preventive maintenance protects both your home and your investment.

According to recent reports, maxson recommends that homeowners have their fireplace professionally inspected at least once a year, even if they don’t use it very often. “Cleaning removes buildup, while an inspection helps identify hidden challenges that cleaning alone won’t solve,” he explains.

Sources indicate that for wood-burning fireplaces, annual chimney inspections are essential. “A qualified chimney professional can determine whether sweeping is necessary based on creosote accumulation, soot, debris, and other conditions,” explains Maxson. “Homeowners who burn wood frequently may require additional cleaning during the heating season” for their fireplaces. The firebox also requires routine attention; ash. Remove ash as needed, based on the manufacturer’s instructions, and keep the surrounding area free of combustible debris.

Gas fireplaces should also receive regular professional maintenance according to the manufacturer’s recommendations, typically including an annual inspection. “Servicing may involve cleaning the burner and other components, inspecting the ignition system, and verifying proper operation and venting,” explains Maxson.

Wood-burning fireplaces should routinely be cleaned to manage ash and creosote buildup. A professional chimney sweep can remove accumulated deposits and evaluate the chimney for obstructions, deterioration, or damage. While gas fireplaces burn cleaner than wood-burning fireplaces in terms of ash and creosote production, that doesn’t mean they’re maintenance free, says Maxson. “Gas fireplaces can accumulate dust, debris, and residue,” he explains. “One of the biggest mistakes gas fireplace owners make is assuming that because there’s no wood or ash to clean up, there’s nothing to maintain.”.

Industry observers note that every home with a fuel-burning fireplace should have working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms installed in appropriate locations. Test them regularly and follow manufacturer recommendations for replacement.

It has been revealed that for wood-burning fireplaces, use properly seasoned, dry firewood. Avoid burning treated lumber, painted wood, household trash, or other materials that can release harmful chemicals or contribute to excessive deposits.

Furniture, rugs, blankets, decorations, and firewood should remain outside the manufacturer’s required clearance areas.

Wood-burning fireplaces can release sparks and embers, while fireplace glass and exposed surfaces can become extremely hot. Proper screens and barriers help reduce the risk of burns and accidental contact.

Sources indicate that ashes and embers can remain hot long after a fire appears to be extinguished. Allow them to cool, place them in a covered metal container, and store that container outdoors on a noncombustible surface away from structures and other combustible materials.

Unusual odors, smoke entering the home, difficulty igniting a gas fireplace, abnormal flame patterns, visible damage, or unexplained soot accumulation are all reasons to stop using the fireplace and have it evaluated. I meant to send this story a bit ago when you were discussing those scary old Milwaukee right-angle drills. Mike really knocked it out of the park with his story about a person spinning under a truck. My story is on par, though I didn’t see it first hand.

According to recent reports, an electrician I worked with had a right-angle drill mishap that stands out as one of the greatest, mostly harmless construction stories I’ve heard. He was standing on an upside-down bucket reaching and drilling upward into the ceiling area with a right-angle drill. You see where this is going, right?

The drill stuck on something, kicked back, and it twisted him off of the bucket. When the bucket tipped he was left hanging by the drill and holding onto the trigger. He spun, dangling in the air, until the cord wrapped around him enough to unplug itself. If I remember correctly, his partner had to help extract him from the situation.

Industry observers note that I sold my right-angle drill to an electrician recently because I hadn’t used it in 10 years due to fear of injury. That was the scariest tool in my carpentry arsenal, not the spinning blade tools.

Industry observers note that are active radon mitigation systems creating radon mines? Does constant suction create defined pathways for more nearby radon to escape the ground? In my 1946 Pleasant Grove, Utah, house I have a partially completed radon mitigation system. It is right now just sucking air from the unencapsulated crawlspace. I’m actively monitoring radon level, and they stay below the 4 picocuries-per-liter threshold while the fan is on.

I turned the radon fan off temporarily. When I finally noticed the radon levels creeping back up, they were much higher than ever before (including before installing the fan). That’s what made me wonder about this idea of creating an easier channel for the radon.

I’m renovating an entire house in Rochester, Latest York, and have an insulation question about the ceiling of a mid-1980s addition.

Recent findings suggest that when I bought the house, the ceiling had Sheetrock with significant sags between the 24-in.-o.c. framing, including one much wider sag in a single bay. I removed the Sheetrock and found the ceiling cavities packed tightly with cellulose, which was weighing down very stretched-out poly sheeting. I also found a roughly 42-in. span with no framing (related to old skylights, I believe). I’ve since had all the cellulose removed and am starting fresh.

The roof is a vented assembly with a ridge vent and several soffit vents on each side, but there were no rafter/insulation baffles. I’m wondering whether there was ever meaningful soffit-to-ridge airflow through the roof cavities.

The existing roof sheathing is also in mediocre condition. There aren’t active leaks, but I expect to replace the sheathing when I redo the roof down the road.

A bench vise is the extra pair of hands every DIYer needs, since some projects require holding a workpiece steady while both hands are busy working on it, and sometimes holding it by hand simply isn’t feasible. This metal clamping device bolts to a workbench and grips the piece so you don’t have to.

Being enthusiastic DIYers, we were excited to test the top bench vises for ourselvesand determine which ones really offered the gripping power we needed. We selected top-selling models, mounted them to workbenches in our own workshop, and used them to grasp boards, pipes, and other items. We also tried out each of their features to determine how useful they would be for various building and installation projects, ranging from woodworking to mechanical uses to gunsmithing.

It has been revealed that after testing, we chose the Wilton 11106 General Purpose 6-Inch Jaw Bench Vise as our favorite for its heavy-duty cast-iron build, slip-resistant jaws, and versatile swivel base. Read on to learn about the different styles and features of the best bench vises and how each model earned its spot in our lineup.

Bottom line: Our tests reveal the best bench vises for various needs, from heavy-duty metalwork to precision tasks, ensuring you find the right tool for your projects.

The following bench vises range from woodworking options with quick-release functions to heavy-duty cast-iron mechanic models—and all excelled in our hands-on testing. The models vary in type, size, and primary purpose, but each stands out in its category. We detail the pros and cons of each so our readers can help determine which best suits their project needs before buying a bench vise. Unfortunately, not all the vises we tested earned a spot in this lineup. The one that didn’t meet our high standards can be found below under “Also Tested.”.

Our Ratings: Mounting 5/5; Ease of Use 5/5; Durability 5/5; Versatility 5/5.

Coming in as our top pick is the Wilton 6-inch bench vise—a formidable workshop tool. Like most bench vises, it comes fully assembled with a cast iron construction; all we had to do was mount it to the top of our workbench. This entailed marking the location of its four holes, drilling the holes, and then bolting it in place. Bolts were not included, which is standard, because the manufacturer doesn’t know how thick a user’s workbench will be.

According to recent reports, we tested the handle-and-screw action of the vise by loosening and opening the jaws and then closing them again. The heavy-duty bench vise jaws moved smoothly and evenly—no sticking or hanging. We then loosened the lever for the swiveling mechanism, allowing us to swivel the vise’s upper portion and retighten the lever to lock it into position. It rotated smoothly to any angle we chose.

In a recent development, the Wilton bench vise has a 6-inch jaw width and strong gripping power—we tightened several items in its jaws, including pipes, iron bars, and wood. We could loosen stuck-on pipe fittings using a wrench without the pipe slipping in the jaws’ grip. We drilled holes in boards, and the Wilton vise held them securely—no slipping. We also used the anvil on the back to flatten a copper pipe with a hammer. The anvil is relatively small—about 4 inches by 4 inches—but it’s suitable for hammering small items.

In a recent development, the downside—and we expected this—was visible imprints in the wood from the corrugated jaws. We could get around this problem by positioning thin pieces of plywood between the board we were working on and the iron jaws on both sides, but woodworking is not the primary purpose for this heavy-duty bench vise.

What our tester says: “This is a general-use vise that can be used for multiple shop purposes, such as holding blades for sharpening and pipes to remove fittings. It can even serve to crack the occasional black walnut if desired—we did that, too!”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer.

This isn’t a vise for woodworking, however. Its serrated jaws are too rough to hold wood without leaving imprints, as we discovered when we used the vise to grip a board as we routed the edge. This vise is best suited to holding steel and iron items, which it does very well.

Recent findings suggest that with smooth inner jaws and a 10.25-inch jaw width, the Yost woodworking vise securely holds large wood projects without marring the workpiece. We mounted this face-mount vise to the front of our workbench, where most woodworking vises are made to install.

According to recent reports, the vise has holes on the inner jaws designed to attach custom wood jaw liners, so we fabricated two wood liners to fit the jaws. That involved routing out sections on two boards to match the size of the jaw plates and then attaching the boards to the inner jaws via screws. This gave us a larger gripping area for holding boards without the risk of marring the wood. Most professional woodworkers will fabricate their own liners for this reason, but the jaws themselves are smooth enough to support many wood projects without damage.

The Yost also comes with an adjustable dog on the front jaw plate that we used in conjunction with a bench stop for holding wider boards securely as we sanded, planed, and routed. We didn’t experience any slipping.

Recent findings suggest that one of the nicest things about the Yost vise is its quick-adjust lever that allowed us to move the outer jaw in or out quickly. This was a significant time saver, as we could move the jaw to fit the board size and then use the handle to increase the gripping pressure.
